full_judgment:
Mahmudul Hoque, J 

1. In this application under Article 102 of the Constitution of Bangladesh Rule Nisi has been issued at the instance of the Petitioner calling upon the Respondents to show cause as to why the Judgment and Order dated 06.11.2002 passed by the 1st Court of Settlement as contained in Annexure-P should not be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and of no legal effect and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. Facts necessary for disposal of this Rule, in brief, are that the then Government of East Pakistan allotted House No. 27/6, Block-F, Mohammadpur Housing Estate, Dhaka by Memo No. 2136-A.O 3L-388/61 dated 10.10.61 to one Israil the predecessor of the Petitioners. Subsequently a lease deed in between the said Israil and the then Government of East Pakistan was executed and duly registered on 2.6.1962. While the said Israil was in possession and enjoyment of the property, the Administrative Officer, Mohammadpur Housing Estate issued a clearance certificate on 14.10.1970 in favour of the said Israil certifying that the allottee has paid entire amount of money payable by him in respect of the house in question. Thereafter the said Israil transferred the property in question to one Anwar Ali, S/O Jumrati Miah by a registered deed of sale dated 15.1.1970. The said Anwar Ali was a Bangladeshi citizen and he was issued certificate certifying to that effect by the Ministry of Home Affairs vide Memo dated 30.10.1978. The said Anwar Ali while in possession of the property in question died in Bangladesh and was buried in Mirpur grave yard. The certificate to that effect has been issued by the local Commissioner of the then Pourashava, Dhaka. After the death of Anwar Ali his heirs obtained a Succession Certificate from the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka on 13.1.1981 vide Succession Case No. 1003 of 1980. The said Anwar Ali after purchase while in possession of the property entered into an agreement on 22.02.1970 with Md.Abdul Bari Miah, the predecessor of the present Petitioners to sell the house at a consideration of Tk. 12,000/- out of which said Anwr Ali received Tk.4,000/- as advance towards total consideration. In the agreement it was stipulated that he will execute the sale deed within 6(six) months after obtaining necessary clearance certificate from the concerned authority. 

3. Subsequently, Anwar Ali received Tk. 1,000/- on 23.1.1974 and again Tk. 1,000/- on 31.12.1976 and also Tk. 2,000/- on 27.10.1978 from Md. Abdul Bari Miah as part payment. The said Anwar Ali died on 19.7.1980 and after his death his heirs admitting the bainapatra received Tk. 2,000/- and Tk. 1,000/- by two instalments from the predecessor of the Petitioners and subsequently they also received Tk. 1,000/- in the manner as aforesaid. After receiving consideration money they avoided execution of sale deed in favour of the Petitioners. In this situation the Petitioners finding no way out filed Title Suit No. 534 of 1983 against the heirs of Anwar Ali impleading the Government as proforma Defendant before the First Court of Munsif, Dhaka for a decree of specific performance of contract. In the said suit the Government appeared and took time for filing written statement on 10.11.1983 but subsequently the Government did not appear and consequent upon which the suit was decreed ex parte. Thereafter the Petitioners filed Title Execution Case No. 7 of 1984 to execute the decree passed in Title Suit No. 534 of 1983 and obtained the kabala duly executed and registered through Court and also took delivery of possession on 10.4.1984. 

4. The Government filed Miscellaneous Case No. 85 of 1984 under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure (“Code”) praying for setting aside the ex parte decree passed in the said Title Suit. The trial Court upon contested hearing dismissed the same, against which the Government preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 17 of 1985 before the District Judge, Dhaka which was eventually heard by the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka who by his Judgment and Order dated 13.5.1989 allowed the appeal and set aside the ex parte decree. Against the said judgment of the appellate court the predecessor of the Petitioners filed Civil Revision No. 592 of 1989 before the High Court Division and the High Court Division after hearing the parties made the Rule absolute and thereby set aside the Judgment and Order of the lower Appellate Court and restored the Judgment and Order of the trial Court. After getting delivery of possession of the suit House through Court the Petitioners through their predecessor Abdul Bari Miah has been possessing the same on payment of rents, taxes and other charges due to different authorities of the Government. 

5. Subsequently, it has come to the notice of the Petitioners that the property has been illegally included in the “Ka” list of the abandoned buildings and against the said illegal inclusion the predecessor of the Petitioners filed Case No. 54 of 2001 before the Court of Settlement praying for releasing and or excluding the property from the said list. The Court of Settlement after hearing the parties dismissed the case by the Impugned Judgment and Order dated 6.11.2002 finding that the Petitioners have failed to prove their title and possession in the suit property and the property has been rightly included in the “Ka” list as abandoned property. 

6. At this stage the Petitioners being aggrieved by the said Judgment and Order of the Settlement Court moved this Court by filing this Writ Petition under Article 102 of the Constitution and obtained the present Rule. 

7. The Respondent No.2 contested the Rule by filing an Affidavit-in-Opposition denying all the material allegations made in the application contending, inter alia, that the original allottee Israil transferred the property in question without obtaining permission from the concerned authority in favour of Anwar Ali by a registered deed of sale and as such the transfer is not valid in the eye of law. Moreover, the agreement for sale allegedly executed by Anwar Ali in favour of Md. Abdul Bari Miah is also not true and the said agreement for sale has been created with a motive to grab the Government property. It is also stated that the said Anwar Ali or his Vendor Israil was not in control, occupation, supervision and management of the case property at the relevant time i.e. on or before 28.2.1972. The said Anwar Ali and his vendor Israil were non-Bengali and during the war of liberation they left this country leaving the case property uncared for and as such the property in question was declared abandoned under the provisions of P.O. 16 of 1972. Finally the property as an abandoned property has rightly been included in the “Ka” list under the provision of Article 2(1) of the P.O. 16 of 1972 and duly vested with the Government under Article 4 of P.O. 16 of 1972. The Court of Settlement upon consideration of the respective cases of the Petitioners and upon proper assessment of the documents submitted before it and the evidences so far adduced by the Petitioners has rightly rejected the application of the claimant finding that the Petitioners could not prove whereabouts of the original owners at the relevant time. It is also stated that, it is the duty of the claimants to prove that the property in question is not abandoned property but the Petitioners utterly failed to establish their claim before the Court of Settlement and as such there is nothing to be interfered with by this Court. 

8. Mr. Moksadul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the Petitioners submit that the Court of Settlement wrongly found that the Petitioners have failed to prove their case in true perspective and also failed to consider the papers and documents submitted before it and on a wrong finding most illegally dismissed the case of the Petitioners. He further submits that Article 7 of P.O. 16 of 1972 and Section 5(1)(b) of the Bangladesh Abandoned Buildings Supplementary Provision Ordinance, 1985 (“Ordinance”) has provided provision for service of notice upon the occupant before declaring the property abandoned and enlistment of the same in the abandoned property list but in the instant case no such notice was issued or served upon the occupant, the Petitioners or their vendor before enlisting the property in the “Ka” list. It is also argued that the Petitioners are claiming the property on the basis of an agreement for sale executed by the owner Anwar Ali in favour of the predecessor of the Petitioners in the year, 1970. Subsequently, the Petitioners got the sale deed duly registered through Court pursuant to a decree passed in Title Suit No. 534 of 1983 and also got delivery of possession through court in the year 1984. Admittedly the Ordinance in question came into force in the year 1985 and the abandoned list in question was published for the first time on 28.4.1986 and finally on 23.9.1986. Since the Petitioners obtained possession of the property in question before the Ordinance came into force and publication of the abandoned property list it was incumbent upon the Government to serve notice upon the Petitioners being possessor in the property in question, but in the instant case before enlistment of the property in the “Ka” list in the year 1986 no notice as prescribed under Section 5(1)(b) of the Ordinance was served upon the Petitioners and as such the enlistment of the property in the “Ka” list is palpably illegal and without jurisdiction. 

9. Mr. Moksaful Islam also argued that the Petitioners acquired title in the property through Court and also got possession by way of execution of the decree and as such the possession of the Petitioners cannot be in any way treated as unauthorized. He further submits that the property can be included in the “Ka” list where the Government took over the possession of the property and Supervising, managing and controlling the same. But in the instant case it is apparent from the papers and documents and the statements made in the Affidavit-in-Opposition, there is no taking over of possession by the Government and as such the enlistment of the property in “Ka” list is illegal and without lawful authority. Mr. Islam further submits that the petitioner got the registered Sale Deed through Court by way of execution of a decree passed in Title Suit No. 534 of 1984 against the government and as such the Government is legally stopped from raising the claim that the case property is an abandoned property. It follows, Mr. Islam submits, that in view of the said decree the Government cannot claim that the property is an abandoned one and the Court of Settlement’s Judgment and Order is submitted to be a perverse one and liable to be declared illegal and passed without lawful authority. In support of his submissions he has referred to the case of Abdur Rashid Mollah Vs. Bangladesh reported in 58 DLR (AD), 20. 

10. Mr. Shahidul Islam, the learned Deputy Attorney General with Mr. Sukumar Biswas, the learned Assistant Attorney General appearing for the Respondent No.2 submit that the original lessee Israil and alleged purchaser Anwar Ali were non-Bengali and they left this country leaving the property uncared for immediate after the war of liberation in the year 1971. The said owner of the property was not in occupation, management and supervision of the property in question on the relevant date i.e. on 28.2.1972 and as such the property under the provision of P.O. 16 of 1972 was declared abandoned and subsequently, the property has been enlisted in the “Ka” list of the abandoned buildings of the Government. In this situation the onus is on the claimant to prove that the building in question is not an abandoned property. The Government has no obligation either to deny the facts alleged by the claimant or to disclose the basis of treating the property as abandoned merely because the same has disputed by the claimant. They also argued that the Petitioners are claiming the property on the basis of a decree passed in Title Suit No. 534 of 1983. Decree in a Suit for Specific Performance of Contract does not debar the Government in any way from including the property in the list of abandoned buildings. It is also argued that the Petitioners have totally failed to prove before the Court of Settlement the whereabouts of the original owner Anwar Ali or Israil at the relevant time. They further submit that enlistment of a property in the abandoned buildings list under Section 5(1) of the Ordinance raises a presumption of law that the property is an abandoned property under Section 5(2) and this presumption will continue until the complainant prove otherwise. It is also submitted that a decree passed in a Suit for Specific Performance of Contract does not mean that the property is not an abandoned property. Therefore, the said decree is not in any way binding upon the Government as there was no declaration to the effect that the property in question is not abandoned property. At best it can be said that the Petitioners got a kabala through Court in respect of the abandoned property and for the reason of having kabala through Court, character of the building has not been changed. 

11. Heard the learned Advocates, perused the Application, Affidavit-in-Opposition and other relevant documents available in file called for by this courts. 

12. A perusal of the documents annexed to the Petition such as the decree passed in Title Suit No. 534 of 1983 and the other documents relating to the property in question show that admittedly the property in question, originally belonged to one Israil who got the same by a registered deed of lease in the year 1962 executed by the then Government of East Pakistan. The said Israil by a deed of sale dated 14.1.1970 transferred the property to one Anwar Ali. The Petitioners claim that the said Anwar Ali executed a bainanama in favour of their predecessor Md. Abdul Bari Miah on 22.2.1970. Admittedly the Petitioners or their predecessor was not in active control, supervision and management of the property till 1984. The Petitioners claim that the said Anwar Ali received part payment from the predecessor of the Petitioners in the year, 1974, 1976 and 1978. Subsequently, after his death his heirs also received part payment out of the balance consideration in the year 1981 and 1983 but the Petitioners could not explain why their predecessor or they themselves awaited for such a long time with a hope to get the Kabala registered from Anwar Ali or his heirs. We have gone through the Judgment and Order passed by the Court of Settlement and it appears that the Court of Settlement in its Impugned Judgment clearly observed that,

“জনাব আনোয়ার আলীর উত্তরাধিকারীদের সাথে বর্তমান দরখাস্তকারীর পূর্ববর্তী দাবীকৃত করা বায়না দলিলের বরাতে বিক্রী দলিল সম্পাদিত হয় ২১/২/১৯৮৪ ইং তারিখে । সরকার উল্লেখিত সম্পত্তি পরিত্যক্ত সম্পত্তি হিসাবে ঘোষিত হয় ১৯৭২ ইং সনে । সে সময় উক্ত সম্পত্তিতে কে দখলে ছিলেন, সে সময় জনাব ইসরাইল বা জনাব আনোয়ার আলী কোথায় ছিলেন এসমস্ত তথ্য দালিলিক বা মৌখিক কোনো ভাবেই প্রার্থীপক্ষ আদালতে উপস্থাপন করেন নাই । বায়না পত্র Execution এর জন্য দেওয়ানী মামলা করেন প্রার্থীপক্ষ ১৯৮৪ ইং সনে । এতে ১৯৭১-৭২ এবং তৎপরবর্তী সময়ে জনাব ইসরাইল বা জনাব আনোয়ার আলী উক্ত বাড়িতে বসবাস করতেন কিনা প্রমানিত হয়নি । ১৯৭১-৭২ সনে সরকার যখন তত্কালীন অবাংগালীদের সম্পত্তি পরিত্যক্ত ঘোষনা করেন, তা করা হয় মূলতঃ সম্পত্তি দখলে কে ছিলেন তার উপর ভিত্তি করে । এখানে Presumption সরকার পক্ষে যায় যে, সে সময় উক্ত সম্পত্তিতে জনাব ইসরাইল বা জনাব আনোয়ার আলী গং দখলে ছিলেন না। চুক্তি Execution এর মামলায় প্রাপ্ত একতরফা ডিক্রি অত্র কোর্টের উপর দায়বদ্ধতার সৃষ্টি করে না এই মর্মে ৪৭ ডি,এল,আর (এ,ডি) পৃষ্ঠা ৭১ প্রণীধান যোগ্য”।

13. The aforesaid observations of the Court of Settlement show that it has considered the case of the Petitioners and upon consideration observed that the owner of the property in question left the country leaving the property uncared for and was not in active control, supervision, management and possession of the property in question at the relevant time. 

14. The paramount question to be considered in the instant case is that whether the Petitioners or their vendor Anwar Ali or Israil was in active control, supervision and management of the property at the relevant time. From the papers available on record, we do not find anything to support the Petitioners claim that the property is not an abandoned property. The property in question has not been declared abandoned in the year 1986, it was declared abandoned under P.O. 16 of 1972 which came into force on 28.2.1972. The Petitioners could not prove that till their taking over possession through Court the property in question was under the possession, control and management of the original owner or their alleged vendor. In the absence of any evidence to that effect the contention of the Respondents-Government stand good. As per law the Petitioners as claimant cannot depend on the weakness of the Government but they are to prove their claim independently by producing relevant documents in support of their claim establishing that the property is not an abandoned property. In the instant case the obligation of the Petitioners has not been properly discharged and the documents produced before the Court of Settlement does not prove the claim of the Petitioners that the property has been illegally included in the “Ka” list. 

15. We have gone through the decision cited by the learned Advocate for the Petitioners. The fact of the said case is a bit different from the present one. In the aforesaid case the claimant admittedly was in active possession, control and management of the property since 17.12.1971 i.e., at the relevant time. But in the present case the Petitioners or their vendor admittedly was not in possession of the property in question at the relevant time, they entered into the possession of the property in the year 1984. Since the property was declared abandoned under the provision of P.O. 16 of 1972, question of service of notice under Article 7 upon the Petitioner or their vendor who were not in possession, active control, supervision and management of the property at the relevant time does not arise. Moreover, decree in a Suit for Specific performance of contract does not reflect a substantive determination of any issue regarding the abandoned character of the property. In this regard the ratio decidendi of the Judgment passed in the cases of CQMH Md. Ayub Ali Vs. Bangladesh and others reported in 47 DLR (AD) 71 and Bangladesh Vs. ATM Mannan and others reported in 1 BLC (AD) 8 are relied upon. 

16. The preamble of the Gazette published on 23.09.1986 shows that the declaration by its own express terms permits of construction to the effect that the properties listed in the Notification have already been taken control of by the government and that the Notification is predicated on that essential fact of control assumed over such property. Furthermore, this has to be read with Section 114, illustration (e) of the Evidence Act, 1872 that permits of a presumption of regularity to be attached to all governmental function discharged in due course. Furthermore, the petitioner could not satisfy the Court of Settlement by producing any evidence that the vendor Md. Anwar Ali was in possession of the property in question at the time of execution of the alleged bainanama in the year 1970 or indeed before or after the P.O. 16 of 1972 came into force. From this, it is to be deduced that the Notification as above records not only the listing of certain properties as abandoned properties but more importantly the fact of these having passed into the control, supervision and management of the Government at the material date in due course. 

17. We have gone through the Judgment and Order of the Court of Settlement and this Court finds that the Court of Settlement considered all the crucial questions raised before it and the Court of Settlement rightly decided the questions considering all the papers and evidences placed before it on the very day of the delivery of judgment. 

18. Therefore, the contention of the learned advocate for the Petitioners finds no merit. Since the property has been listed under Section 5(1) of the Ordinance as abandoned property and the said list has been published in the official gazette the claimant of the property are required to dislodge the statutory presumption as under Section 5 (2) of the Ordinance that the property in question is not an abandoned property and the same has been wrongly enlisted. 

19. In view of the above facts, this Court finds that the case of the petitioners in its entirety is nothing but a castle in the air having no leg to stand and as such we find that the Court of Settlement committed no illegality and find no reason to interfere with the judgment passed by the Court of Settlement. 

20. In the result, the Rule is, hereby discharged, however, without any order as to costs. 

21. Communicate a copy this Judgment and send down the lower court’s records at once.

End.

lawyer:
M.H. Khandker, Abu Bakkar ----- For Petitioner. 
Asrarul Hossain -For Respondent No. 1. Rafiqul Haque ----- For Respondent No. 2.
parties:
Rahimuddin Ahmed  ----- Petitioner 
Vs.
Bengal Water Ways Ltd. and another ----- Respondents.
case_source: In the matter of an application under section 202 of the Companies act 1913.
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.-This is an appeal from a judgment and order of a learned Single Judge of this Court-dated 18-2-75 dismissing a petition for winding up of a Company under Section 162 of the Companies Act, 1913. Petitioner is the appellant and respondent No. 1 is the Company styled "Bengal Water Ways Ltd." formerly "Pak Water Ways Ltd"; respondent No. 2 Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha is the major creditor of the Company.

2. Case of the Petitioner appellant is that he, his elder brother Alauddin Ahmed and his late father Shamsuddin Ahmed had a partnership firm for carrying on Water Transport business. After the death of his father in October, 1960 the appellant and other heirs of his father entered into an Agreement for forming a private limited company to take over the business of the partnership firm and in pursuance of this Agreement this company, Pak Water Ways Ltd. was formed and incorporated under the Companies Act on 30th January, 1961. Alauddin, elder brother and Jahiruddin, younger brother of the appellant and the appellant himself were the First Directors as well as Share-holders of the company. The Memorandum as well as Articles of Association of the company provided for two classes of shares, 'A' and 'B', the former carrying right to vote and the latter carrying no such right to vote. These three brothers held equal A-Class shares i.e. 2200, whereas their mother, Mrs. Zohura Khatun held 6400 B-Class shares. Alauddin Ahmed was that Chairman, appellant was the Managing Director and Jahiruddin was the operating Director of the Company. In June, 1962 Alauddin transferred his shares in equal parts to the appellant and Jahiruddin and thereafter completely retired from the company's business and since then the petitioner has been acting as Chairman and Jahiruddin as Managing Director of the Company. Under the Articles of Association the Managing Director was entrusted with the duty of managing the affairs of the company subject to control and supervision of the Directors. The last Annual General Meeting of the company was held in December, 1969 but since then no General Meeting of the company was called by the Managing Director who began to run the affairs of the company himself ignoring the law and the Board of Directors with a view to making personal gain out of the business of the company at the cost of the company as well as the appellant. No Profit and Loss Account of the company was audited nor was subtitled to - Board of Directors by the Managing Director who treated the company as his personal property. The company incurred heavy liabilities on different counts and its debt rose to such an extent that the company became commercially insolvent. All assets and properties of the company had been mortgaged to the principal Creditor, respondent No. 2, Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha which succeeded the Pakistan Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation (P.I.C.I.C.) against a loan of Rs. 3192 lacs which along with interests and other charges exceeded Taka one core by the end of 1973. The company became unable to pay this debt whereupon this Creditor filed an application for winding up the company but it was ultimately compromised on an assurance of payment of monthly installments which were horsier not paid in these the appellant had filed an application under section 162 of the Companies Act, in 1973 for winding up the company. The application was registered as Matter No. 15 of 1973 and a learned single judge of this Court, in view of an undertaking given by the respondent No. 1, Managing Director, that he would regularize the matter and allow the petitioner (appellant) to discharge his duties in the company's affairs, dismissed the application by order dated June 22, 1973 specifically directing respondent No.1 to implement the undertaking. The learned Single Judge apprehending that respite No.1 who got full control of the company's business might not honor his undertaking gave direction upon him to call the defaulted annual meetings, submit profit and loss accounts of the Company and to allow the petitioner to participate in its management. But these undertakings were not at all honored; none of the defaulted General Meeting were called, no profit and loss account was submitted and the appellant was prevented from participating in the management of the company ; more irregularities serious in nature weft created by respond No. 1 since then Respond. No. 1, with an ulterior motive, filed a suit, T.S. No. 112 of 1973, in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca seeking a permanent injunction against the appellant on the allegation that he had encroached upon the Managing Director's right to run the affairs of the company. Respond. No. 1 called three meetings of the Board one after another in September-October, 1973 not for the purpose of regularizing the matter as promised in the undertaking but to transfer some shares to unspecified persons, but no business was transacted in these meetings because of a state of deadlock prevailing in the company's affairs. Respond. No. I by a notice dated 11-10-73 called an extra -ordinary General Meeting for 26-10-73 to appoint one more Director with a view to come politely oust the appellant from the management. The appellant did not attend the meeting and in his absence his mother Mrs. Zohura Khatun who had ceased to be a share-holder since 1963 was shown to be elected as an additional director by respond. No. 1.There after repent. No. I got a title suit T.S. No. 255 of 1973 filed in the 6th Court of Munsif, Dacca, by Mrs. Zohura Khatun seeking a declaration that she was the lawful owner of 2200 shares and that she was elected a Director of the Company. Respond. No. 1 then proceeded to call a general meeting of the company but at this stage the appellant filed a suit T.S. "No. 259 of 1973 in the same Munsif Court, Dacca to protect his interest in the company and obtained a temporary injunction against the holding of the meeting with Mrs. Zohura Khatun who was neither a share-holder nor a Director. In the course of this litigation in the subordinate courts the appellant, for the first time, learnt that respond. No. 1 had, by fraud and collusion, introduced a Printed Memorandum and Articles of Association of the company totally different from the Company Memorandum and Articles of Association and got it registered in the office of the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies replacing the original one on the pretext of some alteration and amendment therein. Under the amended Memorandum and Articles of Association respond. No. 1-as Managing Director would be the sole arbiter as well as the sole owner of the company having rights to preside over all meetings of the company. Because of this fraudulent replacement of the Original Memorandum and Articles of Association by a printed one the company became non-existent as a corporate entity, its substratum was lost and it turned into a proprietary of the respite. No.1. the appellant the only other share-holder-cum-Director of the company lost confidence in respect. No.1 The Company totally failed to pay its debt. In the circumstances the petitioner filed the application for winding up of the company. 3. The principal creditor, the Shilpa Rin Sangstha filed an application fully supporting the winding up pet t.ion stating further that in case this petition was not pursued by the petitioner the Sangstha would pursue it by getting it substituted for the petitioner. The Sangstha narrated in its application how the company had failed to pay its debt or to keep any of its assurances for payment in instalments of its debts, as a result of which the debt rose to Tk. one crore 41 lacs and some odd by that time Respond. No. 1 then suddenly denied this debt contending that the loan was taken from the P.I.C.I.C. and not from the Sangstha. But suddenly the Snags the played a somersault and filed an application to the court opposing the winding up petition on the plea that the company recognized afresh its debt to the Sangstha.

4. Respdt. No. 1 entered appearance and filed an affidavit-in-opposition denying the material allegations made in the winding up petition, He contended that Alauddin had transferred all his shares to him alone before he retired and consequently his shares increased; the shares of his mother were also given to him and, as a result, the petitioner held only 30 percent of the Company's shares. He, however, admitted that no statutory Annual General Meetings were held after 1969 and that since then no profit and loss account was also submitted to the Board. But he denied the allegations that the appellant was ousted from the management of the company affairs or that the company became commercially insolvent but claimed that it was running on sound business principles and that its assets would exceed its liabilities. He blamed the appellant for his noncooperation in holding the Director's meetings which were called in pursuance of his undertakings before the court. The first meeting was held on 29-9-73 but the petitioner did not cooperate with him; on the contrary, he obstructed the proceedings of the meeting insisting upon the presence of his brothers-in-law in the meeting who were neither share-holders nor directors. He alleged that with the help of his brothers-in-law the petitioner interfered with his management of the company affairs and also misappropriated an amount of Tk. 52,000/- for which he had to file the T.S. No. 112 of 1973 against the petitioner. As to the Extra-Ordinary General Meeting held on 26-10-73, his contention is that the petitioner attended the meeting and in his presence their mother Mrs. Zohura Khatun was elected as an Additional Director; this election was lawful since she had got 2200 shares from him by transfer on 19-9-73. T.S. No. 255 of 1973 was rightly filed by Mrs. Zohura Khatun for a declaration that she was a share-holder and a Director of the company. Petitioner's suit, on the other hand, T.S. 259 of 1973 was wrongly filed seeking an injunction against the holding of the Annual General Meeting on 29-11-73. The Annual General Meeting could not be held on 29-11-73 because of this injunction at the instance of the petitioner. On subsequent dates, when injunction was withdrawn, regular meetings were held and profit and loss accounts were submitted but the petitioner did not attend these. The learned Single Judge on consideration of evidence, oral and documentary, dismissed the petition on the following findings the petitioner stood virtually excluded from the management of the company's 'affairs which lay solely with respondent No. 1, but this virtual exclusion did not affect his share-holding interests; it is, however, difficult to determine whether the amended Memorandum and Articles of Association was introduced fraudulently by respondent No. 1 but the petitioner may seek remedy elsewhere; the dispute as to transfer of shares of Mrs. Zohura Khatun and her election as an Additional Director cannot be resolved in this case but it is a matter relating to share-position of the share-holders which may better be decided by an application under section 38 of the Companies Act. Khondkar has pointed out that the Serial Number of Ext. 1 is "No 1", obviously because it was the first document of the company filed in the Registrar's Office. <u>12. But whether the certified copy is prepared by the office or is supplied by a party comparison with the original copy is a must. Whether this comparison was made in this case has not been stated by the person who purportedly certified it. Mr. Asrarul Hossain has contended that when an oriental document is lost secondary evidence thereof is admissible and it shall be presumed to be correct, as provided in section 74 of the Evidence Act. This presumption is, however, rebuttable, and the presumption is as to regularity of the official act and not as to the correctness of its contents. Again, when a certified copy of the amended Articles of Association was filed by respondent No. I as an Annexure to his affidavit-in-opposition (page 130 on 1-12-75) in the court the last page containing Serial Number One was taken off. No satisfactory explanation has been offered by him as to why this part of the document was withheld Mr. Khondkar contends that the only reason for this omission is that the respondent No. I intended to keep this "discrepancy" out of the notice of the court as well as of the petitioner Respite No .1 subsequently filed the full copy, Ext. 10 containing the last page but it has been kept in the Exhibit File. A document which is the part of a petitions or affidavit in opposition is ordinarily referred to by the court as it is oar at hand in preference to a document kept in the Pat. File. Discrepancy as to the Serial Number of Ext. 10 and subsequent withholding of the last page bearing this number from the court unerringly indicate that the authenticity of the certified copy is doubtful.</u>

13. Ext. 8 as already stated above is a printed copy of the amendment. It bears signatures of the petitioner on every page. No.1. If an office copy bearing signatures of the Chairman had been kept in the company's office what was the urgency for a certified copy, Ext. 10 immediately after registration of the amendment, Mr. Asrarul Hossain has submitted that there is .nothing wrong in obtaining a certified copy of the amendment. "It is possible to come to any such definite finding that such fraud was actually practiced upon the petitioner. No specific remedy in this regard is available in this proceeding under Companies Act while considering the legality or the propriety for 	making any order for winding up of any company. We do not think that the learned Single Judge was justified in keeping the question undecided for this question touches at the root of the mutual confidence of two brothers who were the only two shareholders of the company at the relevant time The petitioner not only brought the allegation of usurpation of all powers by the respondent but also deposed that be got no confidence in the Managing Director of the Company, and if fraud has been practiced by the latter it has cut at the, root of the Company.

Khondker while cross-examining him suggested that this mistake was also made by manipulation as in the case of the missing of the original amendment and its corresponding certificate of tiling. In view of these circumstances we clearly see some sort of a link of events starting from the controversial resolution dated 5-10-62 up to the giving of Ext. 1, as the amended Articles of Association, to the petitioner as late as December, 1975. Even Mrs. Zohura Khatun whose name appears in both the resolutions does not come forward to support them Conduct of the Asstt. Registrar, P W.I. as appears from his deposition has strengthened the suggestion that the impugned amendment under Ext. 9 had been of laced in collusion with some persons of the Registrar's office. No. 1 there is no evidence that the appellant attended that meeting. The proceeding of the meeting were written according to the dictation of respondent No. 1 by his Secretary, T. No. 225 of 1973 for a declaration that she was a share-holder and a lawfully elected Director. No. 1 on 15-5-63 and ceased to be a share holder source then. No. 1 himself admitted, by non-co-operation of the appellant, the only other director, this transfer of share to Mrs. Zohura Khatun was never approved. Under the Articles of Association Ext. 1, there shall be no transfer of shares without prior approval of the Directors requires meat which is totally lacking in this case. Her election as a Director is, as the appellant contends, out of question Resolution of the Board's meeting held on 21-11-73, from which the appellant was absent, shows that her election as a Director was approved by herself and respdt. No. 1.

No. 1 none of the defaulted Annual General Meetings for the years 1970, 1971 and 1972 was held till the controversial election of the additional Director was held. No 1 were not done till the undertaking were given on 22-6 73, no reason whatever has been assigned, Again, no reason has also been given why these "defaulted" General Meetings were not called immediately after the undertakings were given. This is an admission of a state of clear dead-lock created by absence of one of the two share holders cum Directors...It is said that Rahimuddin did not attend the meetings. But, according to Mr. Asrarul Hossain, this is a mere difference between the two or at least Directors, created morosely by one of them and to resolve it their mother has been brought in as an additional Director Mr. Hossain has contended that respdt. No. 1 holding majority of the shares got more voting rights than the appellant and as such he got right to elect a third Director We do not find any basis for such contention. He, of course, got all the 6400 shares of his mother, but these are B. Class shares having no right to vote and as such in voting rights both the brothers got equal number of shares. Under Ext. 1, Articles of Association, there is no scope of casting vote by the Managing Director. Even if we accept the contention that Mr. Zohura Khatun's reappearance in the Company is lawful, her association with the company will hardly make any differed old lady, illiterate and Completely dependent upon respondent No. 1 with whom she is residing, According to the appellant the transfer of share to her and her participation, in the meetings and filing of the suit (T. S. No. 255 of 1972) are all the doings of respdt. No. 1 who says that his mother signs her name in Bengali but the disputed proceedings, Ext. 20, contain her L.T.I.'s. No. 1 did not take any step to undo the "irregularities"' pointed out in his undertakings to the court on 22-6-73; She, of course, called a Board's meeting for 20-9-73 but before that time he transferred his 2200 shares to his mother though no transfer could take place without prior approval of the Board. No.1 who alone managed it He even did not pay the appellant a single pie as remuneration or profit or commission from the company since 1970 in his cross-examination by the petitioner's lawyer respdt. No. 1 stated that he had offered his pay but it was not accepted: but in answer to a question put by his lawyer, respdt. No. 1 said that remuneration of the Chairman or a Director is payable only when he works, meaning thereby that as the Chairman did not work during these years he got no right to remuneration if this is not an ouster from management what is ouster then"?

21. Mr. Asrarul Hossain has contended that there was no trouble up to 1970 but it started thereat tar when the appellant's brothers-in-law wanted to interfere in the company's affairs. We do not understand how a third party could interfere in the company's business if both the Directors co-operate with each other if there were any such attempt action could have been taken according to law. But this subsequent trouble cannot exonerate respondent No. 1 from his failure to do his mandatory, duty to call the Annual General Meetings, Directors' meetings, and submission of profit and loss accounts of the company's business'. Failure to hold an Annual 'General Meeting without proper cause or failure to submit profit and loss accounts even for a year may itself be a ground for winding up a company. But the learned single Judge refused the winding up with the following observations:

"It may be observed that in accordance with the present Articles of Association of the Company the respondent No. 2 as the Managing Director of the Company is in charge of the entire management of the Company as such and on that basis the same respondent No. 2 is running the Company at present-- It may be mentioned that one could see the plight of the Company, it started with three brothers out of whom the eldest brother had left and retired from the Company. The middle brother is in the jeopardy of losing his interests in the company and the company is in the process of getting centered around the youngest brother. In business affairs it is common practice that imbecile persons lacking prudence and commonsense might suffer in the hands of a selfish person with higher prudence, strong commonsense, intelligence and cunningness. But, unfortunately, this situation cannot be rectified by way of a company under section 162 of the Companies Act. The petitioner, perhaps, will have to fall back on some other legal remedy, if any."

We agree with the learned single Judge on his conclusion that by dint of cunningness, cleverness and superior intelligence the younger brother excluded the middle brother namely the appellant from the company's management, but we find it difficult to accept his view that in a winding-up proceeding the middle brother cannot get any remedy but will have to fall back on some other legal remedy. Mr. Asarul Hossain contend d that materials or record de not warrant a conclusion that the appellant has been excluded from the company's affairs and business but he has been misled by his brothers-in-law. Mr. Hossein has referred to TS. No. 112 of 1973 filed by respondent No. 1 against the appellant for restraining the appellant from interfering with his right to management. It has been alleged that the appellant misappropriated an amount of Tk. 52 thousand from the company's cash for the recovery of which that suit was field. This allegation in has been denied by the appellant who has explained that in July, 1971 the respdt (No.1) fled away in the face of a warrant whereupon the office staff reported to him (appellant) that the cash was lying unsafe. He then took charge of the cash, made necessary purchases, such as oil for the company and kept proper account there of and that he did not misappropriate any amount. Be that as it may this incident followed by the filing of the T.S. No. 112 of 1973 only proves deep-rooted distrust between the bothers and the proof of this distrust is the fact that bank cheques of the company's accounts are to be signed by the Managing Director above and in his absence by any officer or servant of the Company named by him, but not by the Chairman.

22. It is the consistent case of the appellant that the company totally failed to pay its debt  which has been mounting taste dilly. 'The company, by mortgaging all its assets took a loan of Rs. 31.92 lacs ( and some odd ) from the then PICIC on condition for repayment with interest in 20 years by monthly installments of Rs. 50,000/- each. The petition dated 15-12-76 of the Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha (briefly the Sangstha) at page 201 of the paper book shows, that excepting irregular payment of a few installments the company failed to pay the debt that installments were re-scheduled at the company's request but without any appreciable result, and that the Creditor had to invoke its bank guarantee furnished by the debtor and ultimately filed a petition for winding up the company Matter No. 123 of 1961. This petition was compromised on a fresh assurance of the company for payment of the installments remained unpaid and consequently the debt increased to Tk. 1,43,00,000/- (One crore forty three lacs) on 30.6.75. When the Sangstha threatened to file another winding up petition respondent No. 2 (Managing Director) met the authorities of the Sangstha and saved the situation by promising to submit a fresh proposal to pay the installments including a proposal for selling out some of the old vessels of the company and depositing the sale proceeds to the Sangstha. But this promise was not kept by respdt. No. 1 who instead of paying any installment or submitting any proposal totally denied the debt taking the plea that the company did not take any loan from the Sangstha but it had taken the loan from the PlCIC which lend could not be claimed by the Sangstha in view of this dangerous move from respondent No. 1 the Sangstha filed the petition strongly supporting the winding up petition of the appellant stating that in case the petitioner did not proceed with his petition for winding up the Sangtha would pursue it by substituting itself for the petitioner. But after a few days the Sangstha filed another petition (at page 214) stating that it would not support be winding up proceeding, but would oppose it strongly citing a ground that the company now acknowledged its debt and agreed to pay it within 10 years by installments, the initial monthly installment being Tk. 50,000/-. Immediately thereafter the Sangstha addressed a letter to the appellant by name asking him to pay the debt which in the meantime rose to Tk. 1.59 crore (one crore fifty nine lacs and some odd).

23. The appellant suspected foul play in this charge move of this Creditor and questioned the alleged agreement for repayment of the debt to which he was not a party. He alleged that the Creditor acted in conclusion with respondent No. 1 to defeat the winding-up proceeding and filed an application to the court to draw a contempt proceeding against the Creditor as the Creditor by demanding the entire amount of debt from him pressurized him to withdraw his winding-up petition which was pending in the Court. Mr. M. H. Khondaker has contended that if a party to a pending case is intimidated or presurised directly or indirectly then the offence of contempt of court is committed and in support of this contention he has cited a few decisions. The creditor respdt. No. 2, tried to explain to the court that the demand notice upon the appellant was sent from its Accounts Office in usual course without any intention to give pressure upon the petitioner and for this act it expressed regret. The learned Single Judge who kept the contempt petition pending till disposal of the winding-up matter dismissed it on the ground that the winding-up petition itself was dismissed and that respdt. No. 2 offered apology. Dismiss of the winding-up petition, we think, got nothing to do with the alleged contempt which should have been decided on its merits. As to the agreement between respdt No.1 and respdt No. 2 for repayment of the debt we meet but suspect collusion or something  like that for defeating the winding-up petition. Mr. Rafiqul Huq learned Advocate for respdt. No. 2 has contended that the creditor is the best judge to decide where its interests lie, in supporting the winding-up or in opposing it and further that the Creditor entered into the agreement as the respdt. No. 1 acknowledged the debt. We are not impressed by this argument for respondent No. 1 all along acknowledged the debt and paid some of its installments. His sudden denial of the debt is a crude attempt to evade repayment. It is said that respdt. No. 1 acknowledged the debt now. What is the guarantee that he would not again deny it the winding-up petition fails. Again, if there were any genuine agreement between the company and its creditor for repayment of the debt in ten years, why the demand, notice issued thereafter? Thus creditor's objection to the winding-up petition does not make any difference to the broad fact that the company dismally failed to pay its debt which instead of being gradually reduced has increasingly multiplied to such alarming extent that in the circumstances revealed before us it is impossible to be repaid. Starting from 1966 most of the installments remained unpaid and as to the position after this agreement for payment of Tk. 1 (one) crore and fifty nine lecs by monthly installments, it is deteriorating as there have been many defaults, as admitted by Mr. Rafiqul Huq, learned Advocate of respdt No. 1.

24. It has been claimed that the company is commercially solvent and that its assets exceed its liability; but when the question of payment of obi arises it is found unable to pay it. The fact that a company's assets will exceed its liabilities is of no avail when its debts are unpaid. In fact, the actual condition of the company's business is not known to anybody except respdt. No. 1 as no balance sheet has been submitted since 1969.

25. Mr. M.H. Khondker has contended that in view of fraudulent introduction of the Printed Memorandum and Articles of Association replacing the original one the substratum of the company has been lost. Mr. Ansarul Hossain contends that excepting the enhanced authority being given to the Managing Director under the amended copy of the company has retained all its character. The objective of the company which was to carry on water transport business has not been altered but under the amended articles of Association the company has been converted to one-man company so far as the management is concerned, if one man Company Law then the substratum of this company has been definitely lost. The learned Single Judge has in this connection observed that though the sole management has vested in one man the share holding interests have not been so vested in one man and that there is a distinction between the sole management and the share holding interest. We fail to appreciate this reasoning for, if the management of a company rests entirely in one person, it will be impossible for the other share holders protect their interests which ultimately will be at the mercy of the one man who will be in a position to purchase their shares at a discount.

26. The learned advocates of the parties have cited a number of decisions in support of their respective connections. We shall consider some of these decisions which are very much relevant to the questions before us in this winding up matter. "In re Davies and Collet Ltd." Law Reports. Ch. Div. (1935), 693 a petition for winding up was allowed on the ground of exclusion of one Director by the other who by committing irregularities acquired complete control of the company, Crossman J. observed:

"I find that the company is a private company in the fullest possible sense and the petitioner and the respondent held the capital of the company substantially in equal shares. On the authorities, particularly in re Yenijde Tobacco Company, I am bound now to consider the petition in the same way as I should consider it if the question arose as to the right of one of the two parties in a private partnership to have the partnership dissolved. That I think is the effect of in-re-Yenidje Tobacco Co. and I think that the principles apply here. I should greatly regret to have to find that the position in law was that a person could be treated and the petitioner has been treated and should have no remedy at all. I have came to the conclusion in this case that in effect the object of the meetings on April 16 and April 18, 1935 was to get sufficient power to get himself appointed managing director and thereby obtain complete control of the company. I cannot help coming to the conclusion that this is a case where it is just and equitable that the company should be wound up".

27. "In re Yenidje Tobacco Co. Ch. Div. 1916 (2) 426 the Court directed the winding up on the ground of deadlock between two Directors who were the only two share-holders of a private company. Rothman and Weniberg had traded in tobacco sale and manufacture seperately; they were minded to amalgamate their business by forming a private company. They got equal number of shares with voting rights: any difference between them was to be settled by a third-party arbitration: an award given in such arbitration was not given effect to by Rothman who then brought an action against Weniberg alleging that he had brought about the merger by fraudulent misrepresentation; they stopped speaking to each other all communication between them being maintained by the secretary; Wenibenrg's petition for winding up was allowed though the company was making profits in the business. Lord Cozan- Hardy M. R. observed:

"If this were a case of partnership there would clearly be grounds for a dissolution and that the same principle ought to be applied; there was in substance a partnership in the guise of a private company. The position amounted to deadlock and it was just and equitable that the company should be wound up."

<u>28. This principle of law of dissolution of a partnership as applicable to winding up of private company is settled and has been followed by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in "Shri Ladli Prasad Vs. The Korana Distillery Co Ltd. (1965) 17 D.L.R. (SC) 52 In that case a petition for winding up of a private company was allowed on the ground of incompatibility and deadlock between the three directors who were the only share-holders. The company was founded by one Kishorilal to carry on the business of manufacture and sale of liquor in the name of "Kishorilal and Sons." He was survived by three sons, Durga Period, Ladli Prasad ad Shanti Prasad; and the business continued as usual till the death of Durga Prasad, the eldest of those brothers, On his death his widow Suruj Muky became one of three directors acting as guardian of her two sons, Ladle Prasad became the Managing Director but he failed to get co-operation and confidence of the two other directors. After long period of mutual quarrel and litigation in civil Courts they all agreed upon a formula of "unanimity of three directors on all matters but this formula did not work and in one meeting Ladli Prasad was out-voted by the other two and found himself ousted from the management. He then filed a petition for winding up and became successful. In appeal the order was reversed but the order for wilding up was restored by the Supreme Court on his appeal. Hamoodur Rahman, J, who delivered the judgment observed. "in the case of a private limited company the tendency of the court has uniformly been to treat it more or less as a partnership and to apply the same principles in the winding up of a private limited company as would entitle a partner to have partnership firm dissolved. Commonly the exclusion of a partner from the management of the firm the existence of a state of deadlock between the partners or the justifiable lack of confidence in the management have been regarded as just and proper grounds for dissolving a private limited company."</u>

29. Next case relied upon by Mr. M. H. Khondker in Loch and another Vs. John Blackwood Ltd.AC (1924) 783 in which the winding up of a company was directed under the Companies Act of Barbados on the grounds of non-submission of accounts and suspicious conduct of the Directors. The Managing Director had preordering voting power; the share holders who were not Directors filed a petition for winding up; it appeared that the Directors had omitted to hold general meetings or to submit accounts or recommend dividends and that they had laid them-selves open to suspicion that their object in so doing was to keep the petitioners in ignorance of the company's position and affairs. It was held.

" the power to wind up the company under section 127 (VI) was not confined to cases in which there were grounds analogous to those mentioned earlier in the section; and that in the circumstances of the case, regard being had to the domestic character of the company, the petitioners were entitled to a winding up order."

30. In refunded Brothers Ltd. 1965 (2) All. E.R. 69' a private company was ordered to be wound up on a petition of one of the three Directors cum share-holders on the ground that the conduct of two directors was oppressive to the petitioner who was virtually excluded from the management. In that case the shares having voting rights were equally divided between the three Directors: the petitioner was ousted from his chairmanship by the majority votes of the other two: the latter then acquired full control and management of a different business firm which was in substance amalgamated with the company but the petitioner had no right or say in that matter; company's bank was instructed to honor cheques bearing signatures of these two Directors only, petitioner's signature being unnecessary; the petitioner finding himself ousted from the management successfully moved the petition for winding up.

31. Mr. Asrarul Husain has cited some cases where winding up of private companies has been refused on findings that d Terence of opinion between Directors did not amount to a state of deadlock particularly when such state of deadlock could he removed by bringing in additional directors. He has also emphasized the fact that a company should not be wound up when it is rendering public utility services to the community or that the winding up will not bring in any benefit to the share-holders )r to the company's creators. In Ripon Press and Sugar Mill Co. Vs Goyal Chitti & others' AIR 1932 P.0 I. it was observed:

"The fact that one of the share-holders has a pre-ordering voice in the company by reason of his owning or controlling a large number of shares is of itself no reason for winding up the Company ultra vireos transaction by the directors is no ground for winding up".

32. In Barron Vs. Potter and Potter Vs. Barron", Ch. Div. 1914 ), 895 there were only two Directors-cum-share holders of a private company but Potter, the Managing Director could not hold any meeting of the Board because of noncooperation of Barron, the Director. Appointment of another Director was felt to be necessary whereupon Potter called an extra-ordinary General Meeting in which he appointed an additional Director, Barron also called a similar meeting in which he appointed another additional Director, whereas, under the Articles of Association of the Company the Board of Directors had the exclusive right to appoint an additional Director. Both Potter and Barron went to court seeking injunction against each other's nominee but Barron's motion was accepted and that of Potter was rejected. In that connection it was held:

"When the Articles of Association of a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1908 gave the Board of Directors the power of appointing an additional Director and owing to differences between the Directors no Board meeting can be held for the purpose, the company retains the power to appoint an additional Director in a General Meeting.

33. In a petition winding up of a private limited company which was formed for carrying on motor transport business A.I.R. 1949. Mad, 675 it was found that three share-holders supported it while ten share holders opposed it and that the company was earning profits and rendering services to the community and that no allegation other than differences between the two groups of shares holders was brought against the company. The petition for winding up was rejected. In  Mahmudur Rahman and other Vs Monipur tea Company Ltd",(1968)20 D.L.R 133 a learned Single Judge of this court rejected a petition for winding up on similar wounds In that case the four petitioners held 16% of the Company's shares; they alleged gross mismanagement of the company's affairs which resulted in heavy loss in business; they also alleged that the company's existing and probable assets were insufficient to meet its liabilities Rut share holders having 84 of the share-capital expressed their confidence in the management and opposed the petition. The court finding bright prospect in the tea industry and in the interest of the majority share-holders as well as of the creditors refused a winding up.

34. In Punjab Ali vs. Muharram Husain (1977) 29 D.L.R. S.C. 185 which has also been cited by Mr. Hossain, the Supreme Court (now Appellate Division) stressed the cooperate entity of a company whose interests are different from that of its share holders it has been observed by their Lordships:

"It is well settled that an incorporated company has got the fundamental attribute of corporate personality which is entirely distinct from that of its members and property of the Company is distinct from that of its members whose only properties are their share holdings."

35. In the case of C. Cooper and Sons, (1937) 2. All E. R. 466, the Articles of Association of the private limited company gave exclusive power to the Directors to register transfer of shares as their discretion. One of the, Directors bequeathed his shares two younger sons but the other two surviving Directors declined to register the transfer of shares bequeathed. Petition for winding up the company on that grounds was rejected and it was observed. "Although if the allegations were true the younger sons might have some grounds of action against the directors in the absence of evidence of improper exercise by the directors of their discretion, there were no just and equitable grounds upon which the company ought to be wound up"

In the case reported in (1966) (1) All ER, 145 Ch. Div. a petition for winding up of a private company by a fully paid up shareholder was rejected with the following observation:

"where a fully paid up share-holder petitioned for compulsory winding up, he must show on the face of the petition a prima Jack probability that there would be a surplus of assets available for distribution among shareholders".

36. Mr. Rafiqul Huq has cited a few decisions to press his point that in a winding up proceeding the wishes of the creditors opposing it should be considered. "In Focus Advertising Private Ltd. Vs. Ahoora Blocks Private Ltd. Company Cases, 1975, 534, the Bombay High Court held :

''If the wishes of these creditors opposing the winding-up are based on grounds which the court considers reasonable then due regard must be given to these wishes. The wishes of the creditor will however be tested by the court on the grounds as to whether the case of the persons opposing the winding up is reasonable: secondly, whether there are matters which should he enquired into and investigated if a winding-up order is made it is also well settled that a winding up order will not be made on a creditor's petition if it would not benefit him "

In another case 1965(2) All ER 761 it has been observed as follows:

"Whether a compulsory winding up order should be made under section 222(e) of the Companies Act 1948 in relation to an insolvent company where a majority of creditors oppose the order is a matter of discretion in exercising which the court has regard to the wishes of the creditors; and reported decisions do not fetter the Court's discretion, but provide a guide only to the considerations to which, grad should be had in exercising the discretion."

In other two cases cited by Mr. Huq Company Cases (1961) 439 and AIR (1971) SC 26,000 the same principle of law namely intending up proceeding wishes of creditors should be given due weight has been followed:

<u>37. In summarizing our discussion above we have no hesitation to hold that the original Memorandum and Articles of Association, Ext.1.was fraudulently and surreptitiously replaced by introduction of a Printed Memorandum and Articles of Association. Ext 10 about which the appellant had no knowledge till the fall of 197. This fraudulent act of respondent No. 1 demolished the appellant's faith and confidence in the company which has been converted into a propriety firm of respondent No. l. The appellant who got half of the A-Class shares of the company has been excluded from its management and also deprived of all benefits from the company including his monthly remuneration from 1970. No statutory meetings of the company were held since then nor were profits and loss accounts of the company's business submitted during this period. Meetings held after the inclusion of Mrs Zehara Kbatun in the company my means not permitted by the Articles of Association Ext. 1 are not the meetings contemplated in the undertakings given by respondent No. 1 as referred to in the Court's judgment dated 22.6.73 but are mere individual acts of one of the two Director-scum-share-holders of the company. The appellant's non co-operation with respondent No. 1 is eroding the Board's meetings in September-October, 1973 resulted in a state of deadlock for which respondent No. 1 was responsible as he had proceeded to transfer shares without prior approval of the 13osrd as specifically required under the Articles of Association Ext. 1. The company failed to pay its huge debt to respondent No.2 which swelled from Celia 32 lees to Take one crore fifty nine lacy by 31st December, 1976. This figure has certainly further increased since then as the company admittedly defaulted to pay the installments even after the fresh Agreement. We have taken into consideration the 'wishes' of the creditor who now opposes the winding up petition. In fact the creditor expressed two wishes, one for and the other against, the winding up in circumstances which have given us every reason to suspect bonfires in the latest agreement for repayment made during the pendency of the pennon. In any case, the agreement for repayment of the debt in future is itself an evidence of the company's failure to pay the debt during the last 14 years. The learned Single Judge though expressed sympathy for the appellant in his plight caused by the oppressive treatment of his brother, re-fused the winding up in consideration of the facts that the appellant would not be benefited by the winding up and that the company has been rendering good services to the General Public. Though there may be good grounds for refusing a winding up in appropriate cases, but we are of the view that these grounds are not available where the mutual confidence of the share-holders which is the pre-requisite of a corporate existence is demolished by fraud or treachery of one against the other. The earlier petition for winding up the company was rejected by the Court on the hope that "the lost confidence between the two share-holders" would be restored thereby. That hope we see, has vanished. This company though, designated as a private limited company, is for all practical purpose, a partnership of two brothers who have now in common only one thing-animosity and hatred. As such, grounds for dissolution of a partnership are applicable with all their force to the winding up of this company. The view expressed by lewdly, a famous author, in his Partnership, p.657, which we share, is quoted below:</u>

<u>"Refusal to meet on matters of business, continued quarreling and such a state of animosity as precludes all reasonable hope of reconciliation and friendly co-operation have been held to be sufficient to justify a dissolution."</u>

38. Section 162 of the Companies Act provides for winding up a company on six grounds three of which are quoted below as they are found present in this case: (ii) If default is made in filing a statutory report or in holding statutory meetings. (v) If the company is unable to pay its debt.

(vi) If the court is of opinion that it is just and equitable that the company should be wound up in view of the reasons given above we are of the opinion that the company should be wound up. In the result, the appeal is allowed on contest and the impugned judgment and order is set aside; the petition for winding up is allowed and it is directed that the company be wound up. The respondents shall pay costs of the appeal as well as the petition.

A prayer for staying the operation of this order in filing of an appeal to the Appellate Division has been made but it is rejected.

Abdal Matin Khan Chowdhury, J.-I agrees.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 23 November 1992 passed by the High Court Division in Writ-Petition Nos.41, 59, 84 and 85 of 1989).
full_judgment:
Bimalendu Bikash Roy Choudhury, J.: These appeals arise out of the Judgment and order dated 23 November 1992 of the High Court Division disposing of analogously four writ petitions, namely. Writ Petition No.41, 59, 84 and 86 of 1989 whereby the order of the Government contained in Memo No. Bhu Ma. D.A/35/81/123Acqn dated 28 February 1988 (Annexure-D) was declared to have been made without any lawful authority.

<u>2. The genesis of the impugned order is briefly as follows: The lands involved in all the writ petitions belonged to one Shah Sufi Emaduddin Ahmed Chisty. The Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka, in exercise of his power under the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act. 1948, hereinafter referred to as the Act, started LA Case No.21 of 1963-64 for acquisition of the said lands for the purpose of extension of Mirpur Botanical Garden, Dhaka. Upon service of notice under section 3 of the Act followed by notices under sections 5(Ia) and 5(3) one Mollah Co-operative Housing Society Ltd claiming to be affected by the requisition, preferred Appeal No.118 of 1964 before the Commissioner, Dhaka Division and the Commissioner, by order dated 21 July 1964, set aside the order of requisition. He found that the notice served upon the said Society was invalid on account of the fact that "the Society was asked to make delivery of possession of the lands on 3-3-64 whereas the order of requisition was signed by the authorized officer and EAC and LAO on 19-5-64."He, however, observed that the order of requisition could not be assailed in any way because it was for a 'public purpose of the highest order'. Subsequently on 22 September 1964 a fresh order of requisition was made, On 21 October 1964 steps under sections 5(la) and 5(3) of the Act were once again taken. On 9 November 1964 Shah Sufi Emaduddin Ahmed Chisty who was also a claimant was called upon to produce documents in support of his claim.</u>

3. In the meantime Shah Sufi Emaduddin Ahmed Chisty made several petitions to the Ministry of Lands for de-requisition of his lands without success. There was also a civil suit, Title Suit No.156 of 1966 regarding the lands in question which went upto the Appellate Division and. disposed of in February 1977 settling the title of the land in favour of Shah Sufi Emaduddin Ahmed Chisty. In the year 1986 some of the writ petitioners and others made a representation to the Joint Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms for either to restore the possession of the lands to them or to issue fresh notice under sections 3, 5(la) and 5(3) of the Act on the basis of purchase from the said Shah Sufi Emaduddin Ahmed Chisty. The Joint Secretary, by his order dated 20 November 1986, rejected the prayer for de-requisition of the lands but ordered for fresh service of notices under sections 5(la) and 5(3)and for, determining compensation afresh. In course of his discussion he observed that Shah Sufi Emaduddin Ahmed Chisty had transferred some parcels of the disputed land on different dates since 1977 in favour of the petitioners before him. The concerned Ministry sought opinion upon the order from the Ministry of Law and the Ministry on detailed reasoning opined that no fresh notices under sections 5(la) and 5(3) were necessary since Shah Sufi Emaduddin Ahmed Chisty had the said notices in due course. Accordingly, the Government in the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms directed the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka to take necessary action under Memo No. Bhu-Ma. D.A/35/81/123-Acqn dated 28 February 1988 (Annexure-D)

4. The writ petitioners challenged the validity of this order. They contended before the High Court Division that since the order of requisition in LA Case No.21 of 1963-64 was set aside in appeal on 21 July 1964, the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka was bound to start a fresh requisition and acquisition proceeding under the provisions of the Act and to pay compensation to the writ petitioners after completing the formalities of acquisition and therefore, the direction issued by the Government in the impugned memorandum was without lawful authority.

5. The Government, on the other hand, took the stand that since the compensation had already been assessed in the year 1964 the writ petitioners who were the subsequent purchasers were neither entitled to any fresh notice nor any compensation.

6. The High Court Division accepted the contention of the writ petitioners and directed that a fresh proceeding be initiated for acquisition of the lands and compensation be paid to the writ petitioners on the basis of fresh proceeding.

7. Aggrieved Government then preferred these appeals with leave of this court.

8. Inviting our attention to the order of the Joint Secretary (Annexure C) and the order of the Government (Annexure-D) Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Additional Attorney-General who has appeared for the appellant, submits that in the order dated 20 November 1986 (Annexure-C) passed by the Joint Secretary of the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms it has been disclosed that after the original order of requisition had been set aside by the appellate authority's order dated 21 July 1964 a fresh order of requisition under section 3 of the said Act was made and on 21 October 1964 proceedings under section 5(1a) and 5(3) were also taken. He further submits that notices under sections 5(la) and 5(3) of the Act are not required to be served upon the writ petitioners who were purchasers subsequent to the initiation of the acquisition proceeding in which their vendor Shah Sufi Emaduddin Chisty was sufficiently notified. In the circumstances, he argues that the writ petitioners were not entitled to any fresh notices of acquisition of the lands in question and compensation on the basis of the said proceeding.

9. No concise statement was filed on behalf of the respondents. But we have considered the pros and cons of the case.

10. It appears that there was a glaring suppression of fact by the writ petitions before the learned Judges of the High Court Division who were led to believe that after the initial order of requisition had been set aside in appeal by Mollah Co-Operative Housing Society Ltd. no fresh proceeding for requisition and acquisition of the lands in question was taken by the Government. This is belied by the order of the Joint Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms (Annexure-C) which was very much before the High Court Division. On this aspect the statement of the Joint Secretary runs as follows; "On 22-10-64 again the orders of requisition under section 3 were made and on 21-9-64 proceedings u/s5(1) &5(3) appear to have been taken. " The Joint Secretary only doubted if the notices under sections 5(la) and 5(3) were actually served upon the parties concerned. It is quite likely that-the service return of these notices got missing during the transit of the concerned records to and from the Anti-corruption office where the same rested for a considerable time. This was noticed by the Joint Secretary in his order. Under section 114(e) of the Evidence Act one has to presume that the official acts have been regularly performed. Nothing was produced by the writ petitioners in rebuttal of the presumption. It also transpires from the said order of the Joint Secretary that Shah Sufi Emaduddin Ahmed Chisty made representations to the Government for derequisition of the lands. He also appeared before the Land Acquisition Officer and made his claim for compensation. And we have it from the order of the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms (Annexure-D) that in Title Suit No.156 of 1966 .Shah Sufi Emaduddin Ahmed Chisty in his written statement admitted that he had received notices under section 5(1a) and 5(3) of the Act. There is no denying the fact that the said Shah Sufi Emaduddin Chisty was fully aware of the acquisition notices. Admittedly the Government went into possession of the disputed land as far back as in 1964 immediately after the initiation of the acquisition proceeding. Therefore there is no reason why Shah Sufi Emaduddin Chisty should not have been aware of the proceeding. The writ petitioners who are his transferees entered the scene only recently and therefore no question of fresh service of notice of acquisition on them arises.

11. Although the writ petitioners have challenged the service of notice under section 5(1a) and 5(3) of the Act Shah Sufi Emaduddin Ahmed Chisty, their vendor himself never raised any objection in this regard. None of the writ petitioners did also approach any authority till 1986 when they made an application before the Joint Secretary of the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms. It appears to us the main object of the writ petitioners was to obtain enhanced rate of compensation securing fresh notices. The order of the Ministry (Annexure-D) therefore appears to be just and proper. In our opinion, the learned Judges of the High Court Division have fallen into an error of law in passing the impugned judgment.

In the result, the appeals are allowed and the common judgment and order of the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos.41, 59, 84 and 86 of 1989 be set aside without any order as to costs.

End.
