Homeland Life Insurance Company Limited and others Respondents
full_judgment:
By filing this application under section 43 of the Companies Act, 1994 (hereinafter referred to as the Companies Act), the petitioners approached this Court for obtaining a declaration that forfeiture of the petitioners 20,000 shares vide the resolution of the Board of Directors dated 16-4-2017 in its 100th meeting is illegal and, also, for having a direction upon the Company to rectify the Company's Members' Register (which is popularly known as Share Register) by recording therein the names of the petitioners in respect of the aforesaid shares.
2. The case of the petitioners is that the petitioners are each holders of 10,000 shares in Homeland Life Insurance Company Ltd (`the Company'), a public limited company incorporated under the Companies Act for the purpose of, inter alia, conducting life insurance business in Bangladesh. The authorized share capital of the Company is Taka 10,00,00,000 (Taka ten crores) divided into 10,00,000 (ten lacs) ordinary shares of Taka 100 each with power to increase or reduce the capital of the Company. The subscribed share capital of the Company is Taka 3,00,00,000 (Taka three crores) comprising of 3,00,000 fully paid up ordinary shares of Taka 100 each. It is stated in the petition that in December 2003, the petitioner No. 1 acquired 10,000 shares from Mr Mujibur Rahman and the petitioner No. 2 acquired 10,000 shares from Mr Sajedur Seraj upon paying off the full consideration money and by executing the Forms-117. At the 36th meeting of the Board of Directors (BoD) of the Company held on 27-12-2003, the (BoD) approved (i) the transfer of 10,000 shares from Mr Mujibur Rahman to the petitioner No. 1 and (ii) the transfer of 10,000 shares from Mr Sajedur Rahman to the petitioner No. 2, and the names of the petitioners were duly recorded in the Memorandum of Transfers annexed to the share certificates. Since the shares in question were owned by sponsor shareholders, it was incumbent upon the Company to obtain the approval of the then Chief Controller of Insurance as per Article 33 of the Company's Articles of Association (AoA). As such, by a letter dated 8th November. 2004 the Company's Managing Director sought approval for transfer of shares in the names of the petitioners, and the same was granted by a memo dated 19th May 2005 issued by the then Insurance Directorate and, accordingly, the shares in question were duly transferred in the names of the petitioners. On 7th May 2011, at the 70th meeting of the BoD, it was resolved that the decision of the 36th meeting of the Board of Directors to approve the share transfer in favour of the petitioners was unlawful and, hence, the petitioners shall not to be treated as the shareholders of the Company. Thereafter, on 20th March 2012, at the 74th meeting of the BoD, it was resolved that the dispute regarding the validity of the transfer of shares having been amicably settled, the resolution adopted at the 70th meeting of the Board of Directors was ineffective. On 18th January 2017, at the 99th meeting of the BoD, it was resolved that the 20,000 shares of the petitioners were liable to be forfeited on account of the petitioners' alleged failure to pay for their shares. On 16th April 2017, at the 100th meeting of the BoD, the Board of Directors resolved to approve the forfeiture of 20,000 shares of the petitioners. Hence, this application.
3. By filing affidavits-in-opposition, the respondent No. 1-Company contests this case contending, inter alia, that the petitioners are not the shareholders of the Company, as neither their names were entered in the Share Register, nor was any share certificate issued in their names; that the Forms-117 submitted before this Court by the petitioners do not contain signature of witnesses; that in the Motijheel Police Station Case No. 11 dated 6-4-2017, which is pending before the competent Court, the signatures of the Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Company on the share transfer forms and on the resolution of the 34th and 36th Board meeting approving the share transfer were found to be forged by the hand-writing expert; that 70th Board meeting held on 7-5-2011 decided that the 34th and 36th Board meetings having been held without quorum, the decision taken therein regarding approval of share transfer in favour of the petitioners is illegal and of no legal effect and the concerned shareholders shall not be treated as shareholders; that 74th Board meeting held on 20-3-2012 decided that if embezzlement of the Company's fund is detected for purchasing the petitioners' shares, then, the transfer shall be considered as invalid and the shares shall be considered as Company's property; that four-member inquiry committee formed in 293rd executive committee meeting and approved in 77th Board meeting held on 31-12-2012 submitted report upon inquiry stating that money was paid to the original shareholders from the Company's fund as land brokers' commission for purchasing the petitioners' shares and the committee made a recommendation to offer to the petitioners to refund the Company's money with cost of fund; that the Company's legal adviser Mr AKM Badruddoza gave legal opinion dated 24-4-2013 for cancellation of the transfer of shares in favour of the petitioners and others and for realization of Company's money by selling the shares in accordance with law and, thereafter, the Company's legal adviser gave legal opinion dated 23-7-2013 for forfeiture of shares if the shareholders fail to refund the money with cost of fund within 3 months; that letters were sent to the petitioners by registered post on 15-9-2013 and 5-10-2013 to refund the Company's money with cost of fund; that Hoda Vasi Chowdhury & Company was appointed as the special auditor of the Company in its 77th Board meeting held on 31-12-2012 who, having dug out the occurrence of misappropriation of the Company's fund by the then Chairman of the Company, submitted report on 14-10-2013; that in the 82nd Board meeting held on 20-2-2014 formed a five-member sub-committee for further discussion regarding the defalcation of Company's fund and recommendations and the said committee recommended that if the concerned shareholders are unable to repay the money, then the Company should offer the shares to the other existing shareholders @ principal plus cost of fund; that misappropriation of Company's fund for purchasing the petitioners' shares was reconfirmed by A. Hoque & Co, Chartered Accounts who submitted report on 6-6-2016; that the petitioners having failed to refund the money misappropriated for purchasing their shares, the Board in its 99th and 100th meetings held on 18-1-2017 and 16-4-2017 ,respectively decided to forfeit the petitioners' shares and transfer the same to the existing shareholders.
4. Mr Imran A Siddiq, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, takes this Court through Regulations 24-26 of Schedule-1 to the Companies Act and Articles 23, 24 and 25 of the Company's Articles of Association (AoA), and submits that forfeiture of shares is permissible only in respect of failure to pay the call-money due on such shares and, as such, the power of forfeiture of shares cannot be exercised in respect of fully paid-up shares. By taking this Court through Forms-117, the audited accounts and the share certificates, he contends that it is evident that the shares are fully `paid-up' shares. He contends that it is the admitted position between the parties that the 20,000 shares transferred in favour of the petitioners were fully paid-up shares. He argues that since the petitioners' 20,000 shares were fully paid-up, the Board of Directors had no authority to forfeit the same under the Company's Articles of Association and the Schedule-1 to the Companies Act and, as such, forfeiture of the petitioners' shares is illegal and void.
5. He next submits that the Company's argument as to the maintainability of the petitioners' present application under section 43 of the Companies Act on the ground of not holding any shares by them is misconceived, for, under section 43 of the Companies Act, it is not necessary for a person to be a member of a company to maintain an application for rectification of the Share Register, as an aggrieved person is entitled to file an application under section 43 of the Companies Act. He argues that in the light of the fact that the petitioners' shares have been forfeited, they are 'aggrieved persons'. He submits that failure to record the names of the petitioners in the Share Register in respect of their shares, being share Nos. 2431-2570, is an omission without sufficient cause within the meaning of section 43(1)(a) of the Companies Act. With regard to the alleged irregularity in the Share Transfer Forms, he places section 38(3) of the Companies Act, and submits that a valid transfer of shares is effected if (1) the Form-117 is executed by the transferor and the transferee, (2) the Form-117 is duly stamped and (3) the same is delivered to the company together with the share certificate. He argues that there is no mandatory requirement in the law for the signatures of the witnesses to be affixed to the Form-117.
6. He, then, submits that forfeiture is not an inherent power of the company, but is a power which is granted by the Articles to be exercised strictly in accordance with the Articles, as because forfeiture of fully paid-up shares is possible only if sanctioned by the Articles or by any provision of law and, moreover, forfeiture of shares is not permissible in the case of loss allegedly caused to the company by a shareholder, he continues to submit. In support of his submissions, the learned Advocate for the petitioners rely on the following authorities; (i) Palmer's Company Law, Page-41.01, (ii) the cases of Clarke and Chapman vs Hart, reported in [1858] VI HLC 632, (iii) In re National Patent Steam Fuel Company reported in 4 DEG & J 46, (iv) NC Sanyal vs Cal Stock Exchange Association, reported in 1971 (1) SCC 50, (v) Kotah Transport Ltd. vs State of Rajasthan, reported in. 1966 RLW.37, (vi) Public Passenger Service vs MA Khader, reported in AIR 1962 Mad 276, (vii) Public Passenger Service vs MA Khader, reported in AIR 1966 SC 489, (viii) Smt Promila Devi vs Peoples Bank of Northern India Ltd, reported in [1939] 9 Comp Case 1 (PC), (ix) Promila Bansal vs Wearwell Cycle Co. (India) Ltd., reported in [1978] 48 Comp. Cases 202 (Delhi), (x) Bhagawandas Garg vs Canara Bank Ltd, reported in [1981] Comp Cases 38 (AP), (xi) In re Bengal Electronic Lamp Works, reported in AIR 1942 Cal 516, (xii) Karachi Oil Products Ltd. vs Narendrasinghji, reported in AIR 1960 Born 149 and (xiii) Dilbhajan Singh vs New Samundri Transport Co., ,reported in [1985] 58 Comp Cases 247 (P&H).
7. By making the above submissions, the learned Advocate for the petitioners Mr Imran A. Siddiq prays for allowing this application for rectification of Members' Register of the Company.
8. Per contra, Mr Shah Muhammad Ezaz Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent-Company, takes this Court through the relevant provisions of the Companies Act and submits that the Board of Directors of a company is competent to take any bonafide decision in the interests of the company if an appropriate or necessary provision is not available in the law or in the Articles of the company, except selling the undertaking of the company and remit any debt due by a director of the company, as provided in section 107 of the Companies Act. He argues that the submissions made on behalf of the petitioners that forfeiture of shares is possible only in case of non-payment of calls and in no other circumstances, is misconceived and not based on a true construction of the Companies Act, inasmuch as there is no provision in the Companies Act which restricts exercise of the Board's power to forfeit shares for non-payment F calls only. By taking this Court through Regulations 24-30 of the Schedule-1 in tandem with sections 17 & 18 of the Companies Act, Mr Rahman submits that Regulations 24-30 of the Schedule-1 of the Companies Act contain provisions regarding forfeiture of shares and a company is at liberty to adopt the said Regulations contained in Schedule-1 of the Companies Act. He submits that this Company has adopted the aforesaid Regulations by operation of law, and Regulations 24 provides for exercise of the power to forfeit a share if there is default in paying calls, but no inference follows therefrom that the share of a member could be forfeited only for non-payment of a call made in respect of the share which was not fully paid-up. He professes that Regulations 24-30 of Schedule-1 have been provided for the purpose of recognizing forfeiture generally and there being no prohibitory clause in the Companies Act or in the Regulations, it cannot be said that the forfeiture recognized in the Schedule-1 of the Companies Act is limited to forfeiture for non-payment of calls. He argues that if the Legislature intended to do away with the scope of forfeitures otherwise than for non-payment of calls, it would have expressly said so. He submits that while Regulations 24-29 speak of the Board's power of forfeiture of the unpaid or partly paid-up shares on the ground of non-payment of calls, Regulation 30 deals with other scenarios when forfeiture of shares is possible in the same manner as can be done in case of non-payment of calls and, thus, in an appropriate case, the Board of Directors can forfeit even the fully paid-up shares of a defaulter member to recover any sum or dues payable to the company and, in such event, if this Court finds that such power has been exercised by the Board bona fide and in the interests of the Company, there is no reason to interfere with the Board's decision. In support of his above count of submissions, he refers to para 28 and 29 of the case of Naresh Chandra Sanyal vs Ramani Kanto Roy AIR (36) 1949 Calcutta 360 ICN 114].
9. By referring to the case of Harlowes Nominees Pvt Ltd vs Woodside (Lake entrance) Oil Co. NL 1968 (121) CLR 483, Mr Rahman submits that the directors of a company may take any decision in the interests of the company so long as they are acting in good faith and they have reasonable grounds to believe that their decision will benefit the interests of the shareholders as a whole, and by referring to the case of Teek Corp Ltd vs Millar, (1972) 33 DLR (3d) 288 (BCSC), he submits that the directors of any company are competent to take any decision for a proper purpose. He submits that in the instant case, though the power to forfeit fully paid-up shares is not specifically laid down in the AoA, the Board exercised the power in the greater interests of the Company and its shareholders after giving reasonable time and opportunity to the petitioners to refund the Company's money that had been utilized for purchasing the petitioners' shares. By referring to the case of Hogg vs Cramphorn Ltd [1967] Ch 254, he submits that the action of directors may be ratified by the company in general meeting even if they have acted contrary to the company's constitution.
10. By putting forward the above submissions, Mr Shah Muhammad Ezaz Rahman, the learned Advocate for the respondent-Company prays for dismissing the case.
11. After perusing the petition and affidavit-in-opposition together with their annexures, upon hearing the learned Advocates for both the sides and on reading the relevant statutory laws as well as the case-laws, it appears to me that the first issue to be adjudicated upon by this Court is (1) whether the petitioners have ever acquired title on the shares in question. And, for an effective and proper adjudication of the aforesaid issue, this Court requires to examine the following sub-issues: (iA) whether they have executed the 'share transfer instruments' (Forms-117), (iB) whether the Forms-117 were duly stamped, (iC) whether the petitioners had delivered the Forms-117 to the Company along with the share script, (iD) whether the petitioners have paid off the consideration money for purchasing the shares, (iE) whether the transferors have ever raised any dispute over the transfer of shares to the petitioners, (iF) whether the Board of Directors has approved the transfer of shares, (iG) whether the company had obtained nod from the Insurance Directorate (defunct), which is presently known as the Insurance Development Regulatory Authority (IDRA), for giving effect to the transfer of shares, (iH) whether the transfer of shares has ever been recorded in 'the Register of Share Transfer', (ii) whether the Company has ever registered the petitioners' names in the 'Register of Members of the Company' and (iK) whether the RJSC had ever received any Return or Document containing the petitioners' names as the owners of the shares in question.
12. If it surfaces that the shares in question were validly transferred in the names of the petitioners without having any objection/dispute from the transferors, it would lead this Court to adjudicate upon the second issue, namely, (ii) whether the petitioners' shares were forfeited by the Company legally. And, for that purpose this Court would require to examine the respondent-Company's allegations that (iiA) whether the money for purchasing the petitioners' shares was paid off by the petitioners' father (who was the Chairman of the Company at that relevant point in time) by misappropriating the funds of the Company.
13. If it reveals that the money was paid off from the Company's fund, not from the fund of the petitioners or not from the petitioners' father's pocket, in that event, it would be incumbent upon this Court to adjudicate upon the issue as to (iiB) whether the petitioners can be made liable for refunding the said money. And if they do not refund the said money despite revealing the allegation of unauthorised taking of the Company's money by the petitioners' father, then, this Court would require to examine as to (iiC) whether the Company should go for charging on the estate of the perpetrator (the estate of the petitioners' father), Or the petitioners' shares should be forfeited to recover the said money.
14. Let me take up the first issue, namely, whether the petitioners are' the owners of the shares in question. It appears from the annexed papers that the shares in question were transferred in December 2003 and in the last fourteen years, no question was raised by the Company as to the proper execution of the 'share transfer instruments' in compliance with the requirements of section 38(3) of the Companies Act in transferring the shares. AlthOugh in the past, the Company did not hint at any irregularity in execution of the Forms-117, however, for the first time in the course of the hearing of the instant Company Matter, it was pointed out that Forms-117 do not contain the signature of any witness. In order to deal with this issue, this Court now requires to examine the issue as to whether absence of signatures of witnesses will affect the validity of the share transfer in question. To address the aforesaid issue, this Court opines that the purpose of taking witnesses' signatures is to ensure that neither the transferor nor the transferee subsequently disputes execution of the Form-117. In this case, since the transferor or the transferee is not disputing the execution of Form-117, as such, absence of witnesses' signatures is of no significance or consequence. Moreover, it is the view of the Apex Courts of all the jurisdictions that trifling irregularities in share transfer shall not be fatal to the transaction. In the case of Re Paradise Motor Co Ltd., reported in 1968 (2) ALL ER 625, 630, it was held that "There is plenty of authority for the proposition that neglect of unessential matters on a transfer may not be fatal to the transfer's validity, and may amount to mere irregularities. .... It is stated (in Buckley on the Companies Act) on p. 811: "lapse of time coupled with recognition of the transferee as a shareholder may render the transfer incapable of being impeached." In view of the lapse of time and Mr Watson's actions in regard to the shares, Mr Watson cannot now he allowed to take advantage of his own failure to procure execution of the transfer by Mr Eric Johns. This can be treated as a mere irregularity ..."
15. Moreover, it is an admitted position that the Company had recorded the transfer in its Register of Transfer of Shares, although the Company had the opportunity to decline to register the transfer of shares under Regulations 20 of Schedule 1 of the Companies Act, read with Article 35 of the AoA. From the annexed papers (Annexures-C4 and C 17), it further appears that the Company took steps to have the said transfers approved by the Insurance Directorate and, thereafter, submitted Form IX (Consent of Directors) and Form XII (Particulars of Directors) before the RJSC. Thus, from a careful scrutiny of the above annexed papers, it is difficult for this Court to hold that the Board of Directors of the Company has not approved the transfer of shares in question.
16. The Company's further allegation that the Board resolution approving share transfer is forged according to handwriting expert's report and, as such, the share transfer is invalid. Given the factual background of transfer of shares that all the works relating to transfer of shares from the two original shareholders (transferees) in favour of these two petitioners, including payment of consideration money, were done by the father of the petitioners as the then Chairman of the Company, the normal presumption would be that the father would not put his forged signature thereon. Moreover, it is the settled principle of law that a handwriting expert's report is not conclusive evidence, for, the Apex Court has viewed the handwriting expert's report to be a frail piece of evidence and, therefore, it does not carry much weight. In the case of Bhagwan Kaur vs Shri Maharaj Krishan Sharma, reported in ILR (1974) SC 10, it was held that "... that the evidence of a handwriting expert unlike that of a fingerprint expert is generally of a frail character and its fallibilities have been quite often noticed. The courts should therefore be wary to give too much weight to the evidence of the handwriting expert. The conclusions based upon mere comparison of handwriting must at best be indecisive and yield to the positive evidence in the case."
17. More importantly, the Company did not produce any other copy of the 34th and 36th Board resolutions claiming it to be the original Board resolutions for the 34th and 36th Board meeting and, further, in the said resolutions the Board of Directors took many other decisions, apart from approving the share transfer, but the Company has not taken any resolution declaring the same to be forged, nor the Company is claiming that the entire Board of the Company, including the Chairman of the BoD, has committed forgery in taking those decisions. Moreover, Form-117 and the 34th and 36th Board resolutions are not the only documents relating to the share transfer. There are many other documents relating to share transfer, the authenticity of which is not being questioned by the Company. For instance, the Memorandum of Transfer of Shares (Annexure-I) records the share transfer under the signature of the then Chairman, which has not been disputed. If the entry in the Memorandum of Share Transfer is valid, there is hardly any scope to raise dispute about the share transfers in question. Also, from other contemporaneous documents of the Company (Annexure-C series) it transpires that the share transfers in fact took place. The argument that share certificates were never issued by the Company does not help the Company to establish the petitioners' claim that they are the owners of the shares in question because, it is the responsibility of the Company under section 158 of the Companies Act to issue share certificates to a transferee within 90 (ninety) days of registration of the transfer. Since it is an admitted position that the transfer of shares in question was registered in the Register of Transfer of Shares, it was the duty of the Company to issue the share certificates. More so, it is also evident from the various notices issued by the Company relating to forfeiture of shares which culminate into forfeiture of the petitioners' shares by the Company that the petitioners were at all times treated as shareholders of the Company. And, finally, since there is no claim or dispute from the side of transferors of the shares as to non-execution of the Share Transfer Instruments or as to non-receiving of consideration-money, it amply suggests that the original shareholders of these shares in question have transferred the shares in favour of the petitioners. The allegations that the consideration money is ill-gotten or the then Chairman of the Company (the father of the petitioners) abused his position in transferring the shares from the original shareholders to his daughters (these petitioners) are different issues.
18. The above conclusion on the issue No. 1 leads this Court to embark upon examination of the Company's allegation that its funds were misappropriated by the then Chairman (the petitioners' father) for the purpose of paying off the consideration for the petitioners' shares. From the annexed papers, it transpires that in the 70th Board meeting held on 7-5-2011, the Company raised the issue of embezzlement of the Company's fund by the petitioners' father. It transpires that up until that period, a group of directors, who are the supporters of the petitioners' father, overlooked the issue and, eventually, when the petitioners were asked by the Company through repeated notices sent by the registered post to refund the Company's money taken illegally by their father from the Company's fund, the petitioners neither replied to the notice nor did they challenge the allegation as to misappropriation of the Company's fund by their father. It further transpires that in order to ascertain, the real financial status, the Company on 31-12-2012 appointed a special auditor, Hoda Vasi Chowdhury & Company, and the Company's said special auditor on 14-10-2013 submitted its report with a finding that the petitioners' father, as the then Chairman of the Board of the Company, illegally took the money from the Company's fund for paying off the price of the shares in question. Again, the Company appointed another Chartered Accountant Firm, A. Huq & Company in order to be confirmed as to the report made by the Hoda Vasi Chowdhury & Company, and it was confirmed by the said CA Firm that the petitioners' father truly misappropriated the Company's fund for purchasing the petitioners' shares. The findings of the Company's two special auditors have never been challenged by the petitioners. On the other hand, the petitioners have never claimed that they have personally paid off the money for purchasing the shares in question.
19. In view of the revelation of the fact that the money had been received by the transferors from the petitioners' father, it was incumbent upon the petitioners either to disprove the Company's allegation as to misappropriation of funds by their father or to refund the money by which their shares were purchased. Had the petitioners pleaded before this Court that they themselves paid the money from their own source for buying the shares in question, the scenario would have been completely different. The only plea taken by the petitioners on this issue before this Court, not during the course of investigation by the Company, is that if the Company's funds had been misappropriated by their father, then the Company should have filed a civil and criminal case against him when he was alive and the Company can still file a compensation suit against the estate of their deceased father for recovery of the allegedly misappropriated funds of the Company. Now, because of taking the aforesaid plea by the petitioners, when it is the finding of this Court that the shares in question were purchased by the Company's fund, and particularly in absence of the petitioners' proof that they have not inherited any assets, properties, cash, stock and jewelleries, the question that comes up for consideration by this Court is that, whether this Court should push the Company for filing a civil suit to recover the sum owed to the petitioners' father, instead of forfeiting the petitioners' shares, at first. Clearly, this is an opportunistic approach of the petitioners, for, while they are not denying that it is their father who paid off the money for purchase of shares even though their father might have stolen money from the Company's account, on the other hand, when the question of refunding the said illegal money is being raised by the Company, they are taking a different approach by saying that it is their father who is liable for refund of Company's money or their father's estate/property should be charged against the Company's claim. The petitioners, thus, are appearing to this Court to be the over-smart opportunistic litigants, who having been illegitimately benefited by their father's misdeeds, now, seek relief from the Court of law. Such opportunists do not deserve discretionary relief from any Court of law, because the scheme of enactment of any law is to let the citizen enjoy a right lawfully, not to allow them enjoy anything by abusing the law in a cunning manner. Since the Legislature has employed the word 'may' in section 43 of the Companies Act ("the Court may rectify the Register"), the remedy under section 43 of the Companies Act is a discretionary one and, therefore, these cunning-petitioners are not competent to invoke the said provisions of the law.
20. In course of hearing of this matter, when it surfaced that the money for purchasing the petitioners' shares in question was, in fact, paid off by the petitioners' father (the then Chairman of the Company) illegally from the Company's fund, this Court asked the learned Advocate for the respondent-Company that whether the Company will rectify its Members' Register, if the petitioners pay off/refund the amount of money embezzled by their father. In response thereto, the learned Advocate for the Company had informed this Court that since the petitioners are the daughters of a promoter of the Company, the Company is willing to resolve it amicably. Then, this Court suggested the learned Advocate for the petitioners to ask the petitioners to pay off the money towards amicable disposal of this case, so as to help this Court to save its invaluable working-hours that require to hand down a full-fledged Judgment. But instead of conceding to this Court's verbal suggestions, the petitioners were adamant to receive a detailed Judgment on the grounds that recovery of money from the petitioners' father is a different issue, which cannot be linked up with the petitioners' shares and, secondly, fully paid-up shares cannot be forfeited. In other words, the petitioners are desperately endeavouring to make out a favourable case on the basis of the technical aspect, in an attempt to defeat the true factual aspect of this case. This Court, thus, finds that the petitioners are merely seeking to take advantage of a superficial side of this case and, accordingly, this Court holds that the petitioners have not come up with clean hands before this Court. On this ground alone, this case is liable to be dismissed.
21. From the above examination of the factual aspect of the case, this Court also finds the answer to the question as to whether the shares were made paid-up from the petitioners' own source or by stealing money from another's pocket or by embezzlement of the Company's fund. Because, this Court's findings are that the petitioner's shares were purchased by their father with the Company's money; not with their father's own money or not with the petitioners' money. Thus, there remains no obscurity to arrive at the conclusion that the petitioners are indebted to the Company for the sum taken by their father from the Company's fund, for, the petitioners have become the beneficiaries of their father's misdeed by acquiring the shares in question, in addition to inheriting their father's estate and therefore, they are liable to pay off the sum due to the Company.
22. Given the aforesaid factual background of this case, this Court requires to see whether the fully paid-up shares can be forfeited by the Board of Directors of a company for non-payment of the sum/debt, which is due to the holder/s of the aforesaid fully paid-up shares. In other words, whether a company is competent to adjust the sum owed to the company by a paid-up shareholder through forfeiting the aforesaid debtor-share-holder's paid-up shares. To put it simply, some examples may be mentioned here. When a company's paid-up shareholder owes money to its company on account of taking cash-loan from the company or on account of buying goods on credit from the company or on account of embezzlement of the company's fund, in that scenario, whether the company should file a civil suit for recovery of money, Or the company should recover the company's money by first utilizing the said paid-up shareholder's share.
23. By referring to a catena of case-laws, the learned Advocate for the respondent-Company argues that the Regulations 24-30 of the Companies Act recognize forfeiture generally and, thus, the Board of Directors of a company can forfeit the fully paid-up shares and, secondly, a company is entitled to take any decision, if the decision is taken bona fide in the interest of the company. And, the petitioners' argument is that the Board of Directors of a company cannot take any decision to impose a penalty on a shareholder in violation of the Articles, as the Articles are an agreement entered into by the shareholders to govern the affairs of the company, and if it is necessary for the proper conduct of the company's affairs to amend the Articles, then, the share-holders may in a general meeting pass an extraordinary resolution to that effect, but without amending the Articles, the Board of Directors has no power to impose a penalty on a shareholder in violation of the Articles to serve the company's interests.
24. Let me now deal with the case-laws referred to by the learned Advocates of this case. On the case of Naresh Chandra Sanyal vs Calcutta Stock Exchange, (reported in AIR 1971 SC 50), it is the respondent-Company's argument that in the absence of any prohibition in the law or the Articles of Association, the Board of Directors has the power to forfeit the shares of the Company. And, in response, the petitioners' arguments are that the aforesaid Judgment is the only authority for the proposition that the Company may make provisions in the Articles of Association for forfeiture of shares for reasons other than for non-payment of calls and, as such, the Company is at liberty to alter its Articles of Association and incorporate appropriate provisions empowering the Board of Directors to forfeit a shareholder's shares for reasons other than for non-payment of calls and, accordingly, the respondent-Company (Homeland Life Insurance Company Ltd) may take steps for amendment of its Articles to allow the Board of Directors to forfeit fully paid up shares of the shareholders and, therefore, in the absence of such amendment of the Articles, the Board of Directors of Homeland Life Insurance Company has no authority to forfeit the fully paid-up shares of the shareholders.
25. On the case of Harlowe's Nominees Ply Ltd. vs Woodside (Lakes Entrance) Oil Co. NL, reported in (1968) 121 CLR 483 and Teck Corp Ltd. vs Millar, reported in (1972) 33 DLR (AD) 288 (BCSC), the respondent-Company's argument is that the Board of Directors has the power to forfeit the fully paid-up shares of the petitioners in the greater interest of the company and its share-holders, even if such power is not specifically provided for in the Articles. In response, the petitioners' arguments are that the facts and circumstances of the afore-mentioned two cases are completely distinguishable from the facts of the present case, as both the cases cited by the respondent-company relate to the propriety of the purpose for which the Board of Directors of the company had allotted shares to a particular entity.
26. Let me be familiar with the facts of the afore-cited two cases. In' Harlowe's, Woodside issued a block of approximately 38% of its issued capital to Burmah and the shares were in effect non-transferable in the near future. Harlowe, a holder of shares in Woodside's capital, challenged the allotment of shares on the ground that it was made for an improper purpose of preventing Harlowe from securing a position of influence in the company or at least without due consideration as to whether or not the issue was in the interests of the company as a whole. Trial judge found that the directors' actual purpose was to give Woodside vastly greater freedom to plan for future joint operations with Burmah and to ensure its long-term stability, and that this was not an improper purpose, even though it had the effect of defeating the plaintiff's attempts to secure control. High Court of Australia upheld this finding. It is the argument of the petitioners before this Court that in Harlowe, the power of the directors to allot shares to Burmah was not disputed, nor was it argued that the directors had acted without jurisdiction in making such allotment; that the only question for consideration by the High Court of Australia was whether the fiduciary duty of the directors of Woodside in allotting shares was exercised bona fide in the interests of the company and, on the facts, the Court held that there was no breach of duty on the part of the directors of Woodside in allotting the shares to Burmah; that the Judgment in the case of Harlowe's Nominees relates to the propriety of the purpose for which the shares were allotted by the Board of Directors and it has no relevance to the facts and circumstances of the instant case, which relates to the forfeiture of fully paid-up shares by the Board of Directors of Homeland Life Insurance Company Ltd in violation of the Articles of Association.
27. The facts of the case of Teck Corporation are that two companies, namely, Teck Ltd and Afton Ltd are involved in mineral resources. Teck had a majority shareholding in Afton, and had prepared a contract between the two companies which would enable Teck to exploit certain mining rights owned by Afton (this was referred to as an 'ultimate deal'). In order to ensure that Afton agreed to their side of the 'ultimate deal', Teck had indicated an intention to remove the board of directors of Afton and replace them by their own nominees. However, before this scheme could be finalized, the directors of Afton entered into a different contract on the company's behalf with another company, Canex. This contract provided that Canex would be issued a large shareholding in Afton. The effect was to displace Teck's majority shareholding and frustrate the "ultimate deal". Teck commenced proceedings against Afton's directors arguing that (as in Hogg vs Cramphorn Ltd) they had entered into the contract with Canex for the improper purpose of entrenching their own position. The British Columbia Supreme Court held that the clear intention behind the Canex contract was indeed to "defeat Teck". However, the Court held that its purpose was not to keep the directors in control. Rather, it was to prevent the "ultimate deal". This, it was held, was a proper purpose, which the directors had a right to use their powers as directors to prevent. The plaintiff (Teck Corp.) claimed that the directors of Afton Ltd, in executing a contract which provided for the issuance of shares to Canex, had acted not in the best interests of the company but for an improper purpose. According to Teck Corp, the contract was a 'colourable device' to prevent it from obtaining control of the company (Afton Ltd.) and that the contract and the allotment of shares were thus null and void.
28. It was argued before this Court by the petitioners that in this case, the issue was whether the directors of Afton had allotted the shares to Canex for a proper purpose, and not whether they had the power to issue such shares in the first place; that in paragraph 6 at page 307 of the Judgment, the Court expressly held that the directors had the power to enter into the contract in question in the following terms:
“There is no dispute that the directors had the power to manage the affairs of the company ... There is no dispute that under the articles of association, the directors had the power to enter into the contract here, and no dispute that they had the power to allot shares pursuant to such a contract. The case alleged against them is that they were actuated by an improper purpose in the exercise of their powers.”
29. It was further argued by the petitioners before this Court that the Judgment in the case of Teck Corporation relates to the purpose for which the shares were allotted by the Board of Directors to Canex; that Teck does not deal with actions taken by directors in contravention of the Articles; that on the facts, the Court found that there was no breach of duty on the part of the Directors inasmuch as 'the primary purpose of the directors was to serve the best interests of the company'; that the Judgment in Teck Corporation has no relevance to the facts and circumstances of the instant case, which relates to the forfeiture of fully paid-up shares by the Board of Director of Homeland Life Insurance Company Ltd in violation of the Articles of Association.
30. The facts of the case of Hogg vs Cramphorn Ltd, reported in [1967], Ch 254, [1966] 3 All ER 420 are that one Mr Baxter approached the Board of Directors of Cramphorn Ltd. to make a takeover offer for the company. The directors (including Colonel Cramphorn who was Managing Director and Chairman) believed that the takeover would be bad for the company. So they issued 5707 shares with ten votes each to the trustees of the employee's welfare scheme (Cramphom, an employee and the auditor). This meant they could outvote Baxter's bid for majority control. A shareholder, Mr Hogg, sued, alleging the issue of the shares was ultra vires. Cramphom argued that the directors' actions were all in good faith. It was feared that Mr Baxter would sack many of the workers. The Court (Chancery Division) held that the directors who dilute the value of the stock in order to forestall the takeover violated their fiduciary duty to the company. The improper issuance of shares can only be made valid if the decision is ratified by the shareholders at a general meeting, with no votes allowed to the newly issued shares.
31. On the case of Hogg vs Cramphorn Ltd. (reported in [1967] Ch 254), it is the argument of the respondent-Company that if a decision is taken by the Board of Directors of company for an improper purpose, the same may be ratified by the shareholders in a general meeting. In the case of Hogg, the issue was whether the allotment of 5,707 shares by the directors with special voting rights to retain control of the company and `manipulate the voting position' a legitimate act on the part of the directors; that the Court held that `the issue of the 5,707 shares with the special voting rights which the directors purported to attach to them, could not be justified by the view that the directors genuinely believed that it would benefit the company... and that the power to issue shares was a fiduciary power, which if exercised for an improper motive, would render the issue of shares illegal'; that the Court concluded however that such improper exercise of powers by the directors could be ratified in a general meeting and, accordingly, the Court held that 'if the company in general meeting elects to ratify what the board has done, there will be no objection to the trustees continuing to hold the shares which they have bought upon the trusts of the trust deed'.
32. It has been argued by the petitioners that the facts and circumstances of Hogg have no relevance in the instant case; that the Judgment in Hogg does not hold that the shareholders in a general meeting may ratify an action of the Board of Directors which has been taken in violation of the Articles, nor does it say that the company in a general meeting can ratify the decision of the Board of Directors which has been taken without jurisdiction; that it merely lays down the proposition that the actions of a Board of Directors taken in exercise of their fiduciary duties, if actuated by an improper purpose, may be ratified by the shareholders in a general meeting; that the Judgment in Hogg cannot be relied upon by the respondent-Company to contend that the action of the Board of Directors of Homeland in forfeiting the petitioners' shares in violation of the Articles may be ratified by the shareholders in a general meeting.
33. From the arguments and counter-arguments made before this Court on the issue as to what ratio were actually laid down by the Courts in the cases discussed above, this Court's understanding on the aforesaid ratio is that in the Naresh Chandra Sanyal's case, there was provision in the Articles of Association of the Company to cancel a shareholder's membership of the Company by forfeiting the paid-up shares for the reasons not related with payment of the call-money, and when the company exercised its power of forfeiting the paid-up shares, the shareholder challenged the decision of the Board of Directors before the Court and the Court did not interfere with the impugned decision. In the Harlowe:s case, Teck Corp's case and Hogg case, the Court approved the Board of Director's decisions on various affairs, as the Court found the impugned decision of the Board of Directors in the aforesaid cases to be either not in violation of any Articles of Association of the Company or the forfeiture was found to have been done by the Board of Directors of the company in the interest of the company.
34. The other case-laws referred to and relied upon by the learned Advocate for the petitioners may now be considered. In the case of Clarke and Chapman vs Hart, reported in [1858] VI HLC 632: it was held that "... If it was necessary for me to come to any opinion with respect to this power to forfeit arising from all these considerations which have been pressed upon your Lordships, I confess that the conclusion of my mind would be that there is no satisfactOry evidence to establish any such power inherent in the system itself, but that undoubtedly, it being a very reasonable and almost a necessary power for parties to have an opportunity of exercising, if it is required, it should be inserted as a stipulation in the agreement." In the case of In re National Patent Steam Fuel Company reported in 4 DEG & J 46: the Court observed that "...The power of the directors cannot be more extensive merely because the contract to take shares is executory, and that being so, the forfeiture was not duly declared, for it is admitted that the directors had no power to declare it. ..." In the case of Kotah Transport Ltd. vs State of Rajasthan, reported in 1966 RLW 37: it was held that "A bare perusal of Article 29 would show that it can come into play in a case where any member fails to pay any call or instalment on or before the date appointed for the payment of the same. So, it was only in the case of member's failure to pay call or instalment on or before the appointed date for payment that the Directors were authorized to issue a notice requiring such member to pay the same together with interest. Similarly it is clear from the language of Article 34A that the provision regarding forfeiture could apply in the case of non-payment of any sum which by the terms of the issue of the share became payable at a fixed time ... In clause 4 it was provided that the grantee shall allot to His Highness's Government fully paid up shares to the value of one lakh rupees free of cost. ... It is clear from the language of this clause that it was never in the contemplation of the parties to the covenant that the grantor would ever be required to pay any call or instalment in respect of these shares." In the case of Public Passenger Service vs MA Khader, reported in AIR 1962 Mad 276: the Court held that "The articles of a company generally contain provisions for the forfeiture of shares for non-payment of calls or instalments. The power of forfeiting the shares is not inherent in a company. It only exists where it is given by the articles or introduced into them as it may be by a special resolution. ... Forfeiture being a penalty and sometime a very severe one, the greatest care should be taken to comply exactly and strictly with all the provisions relating to it in the articles. Any irregularity in the procedure or any departure from the rules laid down however slight will as against the company invalidate the forfeiture." In the case of Smt Premila Devi vs Peoples Bank of Northern India Ltd., reported in [1939] 9 Comp Case 1 (PC), the Court held that "In the matter of the forfeiture of shares, technicalities must be strictly observed. ... Where the power of a company to forfeit shares has arisen, the articles of association usually contain provisions as to the sending of notices and the like that may be regarded as being inserted merely for the protection of the shareholder affected. Such provisions may properly be regarded as being directory only and capable of being waived by the individual shareholder. But no waiver by him can confer upon the company or its directors a power of forfeiture that they do not possess, as for example, a power to forfeit shares for non-payment of calls that are not yet due." In the case of Promila Bansal vs Wearwell Cycle Co. (India) Ltd., reported in [1978] 48 Comp. Cases 202 (Delhi): the Court held that "In the case of forfeiture of shares, technicalities must be strictly observed and a very little -inaccuracy in complying with the conditions precedent to a forfeiture is, as against the company, as fatal as the greatest." In the case of Bhagawandas Garg vs Canara Bank Ltd., reported in [1981] Comp Cases 38 (AP): the Court observed that "... Service of such notice is a condition precedent to be fulfilled by the company before forfeiture of the shares, and any irregularity committed in the service of such notice is fatal to the validity of the forfeiture." In the case of In re Bengal Electronic Lamp Works, reported in AIR 1942 Cal 516: the Court observed that "In the case of forfeiture of the shares of a shareholder by the company, a strict adherence to the provisions of a contract between the company and the shareholders is necessary. No forfeiture of shares can be made unless every condition precedent has been strictly and literally complied with, a very little inaccuracy being as fatal as the greatest." In the case of Karachi Oil Products Ltd. vs Narendra-singhji, reported in AIR 1960 Bom 149: the Court held that "It is also clear that forfeiture is treated very strictly by the Courts, and the directors seeking to enforce it must exactly pursue the course of procedure marked out by the articles. A slight irregularity is as fatal as the greatest. Thus if the call in respect of which the forfeiture is made was not validly made or if the notice on which the forfeiture is founded is inaccurate in requiring payment of interest from a wrong date ..., the forfeiture may be held invalid." In the case of Dilbhajan Singh vs New Samundri Transport Co., reported in [1985] 58 Comp Cases 247 (P&H): the Court held that "... Moreover the company may have some grudge against a particular shareholder if he has caused some loss to the company, but forfeiture of shares of all the shareholders without finding out or determining the individual liability and without giving separate notice to all of them would certainly be illegal and improper. There is nothing on record to show as to which individual shareholder was responsible for causing the loss, or whether the loss had occurred as a result of mismanagement or was it a loss in the ordinary course of business."
<u>35. The cumulative judicial pronouncements and dicta, as emerge from the ratios and observations laid down in the above-mentioned cases, are that if there is a provision of forfeiture of shares in any statutory law or in the Articles of Association containing the procedures of forfeiting the shares, the Board of Directors of a company must exhaust the procedural formalities in forfeiting the shares, for, the power to forfeit share of a shareholder is considered by the Courts to be a draconian power, which is why, the Courts are always in favour of seeing that whenever Articles of Association of a company empowers its Board of Directors to forfeit an unpaid/paid-up share, the said power is being exercised by the Board of Directors of a company upon observing all the formalities of natural justice, that is to say, after being confirmed that the notice has been received by the person whose share is being proposed to be forfeited and, thereafter, the said shareholder has also been afforded an opportunity to resist the forfeiture either by paying off the money due or by complying with the BoD's directives, as the case may be, and the aforesaid duty of the Board of Directors of a company is more onerous if it wants to forfeit the paid-up shares.</u>
36. In this case the paid-up shares have been forfeited by the Board of Directors on the ground that the paid-up shareholders owe money to the company and, thus, the issue to be adjudicated upon by this Court is whether a paid-up share can be forfeited on the ground of non-payment of the company's money. Since the preponderance of authorities on the Company Law, such as, (1) Gore-Browne on Companies, (2) Palmer's Company Law, (3) Halsbury's Laws of England and (4) Penington's Company Law propounds that a company does not possess inherent power to forfeit any share, be it paid-up or unpaid, and it only exists where it is given by the Company's Articles or by any law of the land, I need to find out whether there is any provision of forfeiture in our Companies Act or in the Articles of Association of this Company. Upon skimming through the whole Companies Act, it transpires that there is no provision permitting forfeiture of the shares, but the word "forfeiture" appears in section 36(2)(c)(7) of the Companies Act, in Regulations 24 to 30 of the Schedule to the Companies Act, in clauses 14 (a) of the Schedule X and in clause 9 of the Schedule XI to the Companies Act. The aforesaid provisions of section 36, Schedules X and XI to the Companies Act contain the word "forfeiture" in general terms without any qualification whatsoever. So, a company is at liberty to incorporate the provisions for forfeiture of shares, be it paid-up or unpaid on the ground to be stated in the Articles of Association without offending against any provisions of the Companies Act or the general law of the land. For example, if the provision of forfeiture in the Articles of Association amounts to reduction of share capital or purchase of shares of the company by itself, then, the Board of Directors is prohibited from exercising the said power without the approval of the Court. Since Regulations 24 to 30 of the Schedule-1 to the Companies Act is a full Chapter containing the provisions for forfeiture of the shares, it would be profitable to look at the aforesaid provisions, which are reproduced below:
Forfeiture of shares:
24. If a member fails to pay any call or installment of a call on the day appointed for payment of thereof, the directors may, at any time thereafter as any part of such call or installment remain unpaid, serve a notice on him requiring payment of so much of the call or installment as is unpaid, together with any interest which may have accrued.
25. The notice shall name a further day, not earlier than the expiration of fourteen days from the date of the notice, on or before which the payment required by the notice is to be made, and shall state that in the event of non-payment or before the time so appointed, the shares in respect of which the call was made will be liable to be forfeited.
26. If the requirements of any such notice as aforesaid are not complied with, any share in respect of which the notice has been given may, at any time thereafter but before the payment required by the notice has been made be forfeited by a resolution of the directors to that effect.
27. A forfeited share may be sold or otherwise disposed of on such terms and in such manner as the directors think fit and at any time before a sale or disposition, the forfeiture may be cancelled on such terms as the directors think fit.
28. A person whose shares have been forfeited shall cease to be a member in respect of the forfeited shares but shall, notwithstanding, remain liable to pay to the company all moneys which at the date of forfeiture, were presently payable by him to the company in respect of the shares, but his liability shall cease if and when the company received payment in full of the nominal amount of the shares.
29. (1) A duly verified declaration in writing that the declarant is a director of the company, and that a share in the company has been duly forfeited on a date stated in the declaration, shall be conclusive evidence of the facts therein stated as against all persons claiming to be entitled to the share.
(2) Such declaration, and the receipt of the company for the consideration if any, given for the share on the sale or disposition thereof, shall constitute a good title to the share.
(3) The person who becomes the shareholder under sub-regulation (2) shall be registered as the holder of the share and shall not be bound to see to the application of the purchase-money, if any, nor shall his title to the share be affected by any irregularity or invalidity in the proceedings in reference to the forfeiture, sale or disposal of the share.
30. The provisions of these regulations as to forfeiture shall apply in the case of non-payment of any sum which, by the terms of issue of a share, become payable at a fixed time, whether on account of the amount of the share, or by way of premium, as if the same has been  payable by virtue of a call duly made and notified.
37. The above provisions of the Schedule-1 to the Companies Act have become the integral parts of the Articles of Association (AoA) of the respondent-Company by operation of sections 2(1)(a), 17 and 18 of the Companies Act, because under section 2(1)(a) of the Companies Act, `Articles' means the Articles of Association of a company including, so far as they apply to the company, the Regulations contained in Schedule-1 to the Companies Act, and section 18 of the Companies Act says that in case of a company limited by shares and registered after the commencement of the Act, if Articles are not registered, or if Articles are registered, in so far as the Articles do not exclude or modify the Regulations in Schedule-1, those Regulations shall, so far as applicable, be the Regulations of the company in the same manner and to the same extent as if they were contained in the duly registered Articles. Evidently, the Articles of Association of the Company has not excluded the provisions of Regulations 24-30 of the Schedule-1 to the Companies Act and, thus, in the absence of any exclusion clause, the Regulations 24-30 of Schedule-1 to the Companies Act have become/ formed part of the Articles of Association (AoA) of the respondent-Company by operation of law.
38. By applying the above provisions of the Company's AoA, let me see whether the Company was competent to forfeit fully paid-up shares, albeit the shares were made paid-up by ill-gotten money. From a plain perusal of the above provisions, it appears to this Court that by virtue of Regulations 24 of the Companies Act, when a company adopts it as its Article, the company becomes empowered to, forfeit the unpaid shares in the event of failure of the shareholder to pay any call or instalment of a call within a time stipulated in the notice sent by the company, and by dint of Regulations 30 of the Companies Act, if it is adopted by a company, the company becomes empowered to forfeit shares for non-payment of any sum which has become payable at a fixed-time as per the terms of issue of share, such as payment of a sum as premium, despite receiving notice from the company.
39. In my view, the wordings employed in the provisions of Regulations 30 of the Companies Act are sufficient to imply that the paid-up shares may be forfeited in the same manner as is applicable for the unpaid shares for recovery of a sum due to the paid-up shareholders. Thus, this Court holds that since the Articles of Association of the Company contains provisions as to forfeiture of unpaid shares as well as forfeiture of share for non-payment any other sum, the Company was competent to take the decision to forfeit the petitioners' paid-up shares. Further, since it transpires from the annexed papers that the Company observed all the formalities of natural justice before forfeiting the shares in question, i.e. the Company issued notices upon the petitioners by registered posts on a number of occasions as well as published notices in the daily national newspapers and, thereafter, waited considerably a long time for the petitioners' reply, this Court finds that the impugned decision has not been taken in violation of Articles of Association of the Company. It is to be mentioned here that since the Company has decided to allocate the forfeited shares among the existing shareholders, there shall not be any reduction of capital if the shares are transferred at a par value. In other words, since the shares are paid-up shares and if the shares are transferred in consideration of the money which are currently a shortfall of the Company's fund (the amount of money which has been. defalcated by the then Chairman of the Company), then, there shall not be any reduction. But if the shares are transferred at a consideration-money less than the amount of money defalcated by the then Chairman of the Company, it shall result in a reduction in share capital and, in that case, the Company must take approval from this Court. Also, if the Company fails to dispose of the forfeited shares within a stipulated time, the Company shall be under an obligation to cancel the shares in question and, then, take approval of this Court.
<u>40. The summary of the findings and observations made hereinbefore by this Court may be recorded, for convenience, in the following language:</u>
<u>(i) The petitioners' shares in question were purchased by their father upon embezzlement of the Company's fund. In other words, they acquired the shares in question by ill-gotten money. It is, thus, held that although the petitioners utilized the aforesaid illegal money for paying off the consideration-money in purchasing the shares in question, nevertheless, the petitioners became the owners of the shares in question.</u>
<u>(ii) The petitioners are liable to refund the Company's said money, which have been illegally taken by their father for purchasing the shares in question. In other words, since the petitioners owe the said money to the Company, they must refund/pay off the same to the Company.</u>
<u>(iii) In the scheme of our Companies Act, forfeiture is permitted subject to compliance with the provisions regarding reduction of share capital of a company. But the power of forfeiture by a company can be exercised only if the same is provided/contained in the Articles of Association of a company, either in specific terms or in general terms.</u>
<u>(iv) The Board of Directors of a company must be considerate in exercising the power of forfeiture in a very rare situation where the Board of Directors would genuinely believe that the forfeiture is required in the interest of the company. And, when the Board of Directors decides to forfeit the shares, it must observe the Rules of natural justice.</u>
<u>(v) This Court is of the view that the Regulations 24-30 of the Companies Act, having become part of the Articles of Association of the Company by operation of law, empowers this Company to forfeit not only the unpaid shares for the shareholder's failure to pay the call-money, but also for recovery of the sum due to a paid-up shareholder. Given this Court's findings that the petitioners are the debtors to the Company, this Court holds that the impugned decision of the Board of Directors of the Company as to the forfeiture of shares was rightly taken by the Board of Directors of the Company.</u>
<u>(vi) Given the findings of this Court that these petitioners have acquired the shares of the Company by embezzlement of the Company's fund, now, if this Court compels the Company to recover the money through filing any civil suit, it would amount to granting undue benefit to a law-violator. Further, since it has been held by this Court that after the petitioners' father's death, they not only have acquired the shares in question by their father's misdeed, but they also have inherited their father's other properties, therefore, it would be irrational to ask the Company to approach the civil Court for reimbursement of the defalcated money from their father's property.</u>
<u>(vii) Since the Company has showed its willingness to resolve the dispute amicably on the condition of receiving the entire amount of the Company's money with cost, therefore, the petitioners are hereby given an opportunity to retain the shares in question by refunding the Company's fund to the respondent-Company with 6% interest within 2 (two) months from the date of receipt of this Judgment and Order.</u>
<u>(viii) If the petitioners do not pay off/refund the money within the stipulated time, the Company shall be competent to allocate the shares in question among the present shareholders in consideration of the amount of money defalcated by the then Chairman plus 6% interest per annum.</u>
<u>(ix) If the Company fails to dispose of the shares in question within 3 (three) months from the date of receipt of this Order, in that event, the Company must take a resolution for cancellation of these shares and approach this Court for obtaining an approval thereto.</u>
41. In the result, this application under section 43 of the Companies Act is dismissed with a direction upon the Company that if the petitioners refund/pay off the Company's fund (the amount of money shown to have been paid off to the original shareholders, namely, Mr Mujibur Rahman and Mr Sajedur Rahman for purchasing shares from them in the names of these two petitioners) within two months from the receipt of this Judgment and Order, their names shall be recorded in the Company's Members' Register (Share Register).
42. Before parting with this Judgment, I find it appropriate to jot down that the learned Advocate for the petitioner Mr Imran A. Siddiq and the learned Advocate for the respondent-Company Mr Shah Mohammad Ezaz Rahman, in the backdrop of insufficiency of the statutory laws as well as case-laws on the laws of forfeiture, carried out an extensive research in an endeavour to assist this Court in adjudicating upon the relevant issues of this case exhaustively by making available a bunch of case-laws of a number of foreign jurisdictions, such as, UK, USA, Australia, Canada and India. This Court acknowledges that the assistance rendered by these two promising Advocates was truly useful to comfortably dispose of this case.
43. The Company will donate Taka 10,00,000 (ten lacs) only through Pay Order, out of which (1) Taka 1,00,000 (one lac) to Anujani Zame Masjid and Pathagar, Chatak, Sunamgonj, (2) Taka 1,00,000 (one lac) to Deurpar Chandra Jame Masjid, Deurpar Chandra, Jamalpur, (3) Taka 1,00,000 (one lac) to Charigram Khandakerhati, Baghuria Jame Mosjid, Mithamoin, Kishorgonj, (4) Taka 1,00,000 (one lac) to Romanathpur Mollapara Jame Masjid, Khoksha, Kustia, (5) Taka 50,000 (fifty thousand) to Baitul Hakim Jame Masjid, Basherpul, Demra, Dhaka-1362, (6) Taka 50,000 (fifty thousand) to Professor Para Jame Masjid, Birampur, Dinajpur, (7) Taka 50,000 (fifty thousand) to Nuthurchar Eidgah Moydan, Gopalpur, Tangail, (8) Taka 50,000 (fifty thousand) to Thanapara Zameya Masjid, Thanapara, Lalmonirhat, (9) Taka 50,000 (fifty thousand) to Putina Kendrio Jame Masjid, Rupganj, Narayangonj, (10) Taka 50,000 (fifty thousand) to Dorun Bali Jame Masjid, Netrokona Sador, Netrokona, (11) Taka 50,000 (fifty thousand) to Sree Ramkrisno Sebasrom, Badorgonj, Rangpur, (12) Taka 50,000 (fifty thousand) to Muktarpur Jame Masjid, Salla, Sunamganj, (13) Taka 50,000 (fifty thousand) to Mamudnagor Sorbajoya Puja Mondir, Salla, Sunamganj, (14) Taka 50,000 (fifty thousand) to Baitul Aman Jame Masjid  O Madrasha, Mymenshing Sador, Mymenshing, (15) Taka 30,000 (thirty thousand) to Paschimgaon Soa Soyani Jame Masjid, Laksham, Cumilla, (16) Taka 20,000 (twenty thousand) to Al-Nur Jame Masjid, Laksham, Cumilla, (17) Taka 25,000 (twenty five thousand) to Raniad Ferdousgonj Gorasthan Hafizia Madrasha, Raniad, Madhupur, Tangail and (18) Taka 25,000 (twenty five thousand) to Kagasura Dewan Muslim Gorosthan, Vill: Kagasura, 3 No. Chorbariya Union, Barisal Sadar, Barisal. On furnishing receipts of payments, the Order may be drawn up, if so prayed for.

full_judgment:
At the instance of the petitioner, this Court was pleased to issue Rule with the following terms:
"Records need not be called for. Let a Rule be issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 1-4-2021 passed by the learned Senior District Judge, Satkhira in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 5 of 2021 allowing the same as modified way by reversing the order No. 6 dated 13-12-2020 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Ashashuni, Satkhira in Title Suit No. 114 of 2020 rejecting the application under Section 39 Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure filed by the plaintiff-appellant-opposite party No. 1 should not be set-aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper."
2. Facts leading to the issuance of the Rule are inter alia that the opposite party No. 1 being plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 114 of 2020 before the Court of the learned Assistant Judge, Ashashuni, Satkhira with the following relief:
“গত ইং ১০-১১-২০২০ তারিখের কুন্দুড়িয়া সরকারী প্রাথমিক বিদ্যালয়ের অভিভাবক সদস্য পদে নির্বাচনের জন্য প্রকাশিত বিজ্ঞপ্তি সম্পূর্ণ অন্যায়, বেআইনী, তঞ্চকী, যোগসাজসী এবং নীতিমালা বহির্ভূত প্রচার বাবদ বাদীপক্ষ বিবাদীপক্ষের বিরুদ্ধে ডিক্রী পান।"
3. The plaintiff also filed an application under Order XXXIX, rule 1 & 2 for temporary injunction. The defendant entered appearance in the suit by filing written objection and denied the materials allegation set out in the injunction petition. Upon hearing, the learned Assistant Judge was pleased to dismiss the injunction petition. Questioning the legality and propriety of the judgment and order of the learned Assistant Judge, the plaintiff preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 5 of 2021 before the Court of the learned Senior District Judge, Satkhira. Upon hearing, the learned Senior District Judge was pleased to allow the same with some modifications the judgment and order of the learned Assistant Judge. Challenging the chastity of the judgment and order of the learned Senior District Judge, the petitioner moved this Court and obtained the aforesaid Rule, stay and status quo therewith.
4. Heard the submissions advanced by the learned Advocates for the petitioner and the opposite party No. 1 and perused the entire materials on record with care and attention and seriousness as they deserve. The convoluted question of law embroiled in this case has meticulously been waded through.
5. The learned Assistant Judge after assigning cogent reason was pleased to reject the petition for temporary injunction. In this respect, the relevant portion of the judgment of the learned Assistant Judge may be read as follows:
"বাদীপক্ষের নিষেধাজ্ঞার দরখাস্ত, উক্ত দরখাস্তের প্রেক্ষিতে বিবাদীপক্ষের লিখিত আপত্তিসহ দাখিলী কাগজাদিসহ নথি পর্যালোচনা করিলাম।
বাদীপক্ষ দাতা সদস্য হিসেবে অত্র মামলা দাখিল করেছেন এবং গত ইং ১০-১১-২০২০ তারিখের বিজ্ঞপ্তি ��নুসারে কোন কার্যক্রম করতে না পারে, সে মর্মে ১ এবং ২ নং বিবাদীপক্ষের বিরুদ্ধে অস্থায়ী নিষেধাজ্ঞার দরখাস্ত করেছেন। ১ নং বিবাদী হিসেবে সহকারী উপজেলা শিক্ষা অফিসার তার আপত্তিতে উল্লেখ করেছেন যে, ২ নং বিবাদী ২০-৬-২০২০ ইং তারিখে অভিভাবক সদস্য নির্বাচন করেন। এই নির্বাচনের বিষয়ে জানতে পেরে ৯-৭-২০ ইং তারিখে উপজেলা নির্বাহী অফিসারের নিকট আবেদন করলে উপজেলা নির্বাহী অফিসার ২৮-৭-২০ ইং তারিখে উপজেলা শিক্ষা কর্মকর্তা বরাবর ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণের জন্য প্রেরণ করেন। উপজেলা শিক্ষা কর্মকর্তা উক্ত বিষয়ে ১ নং বিবাদীকে তদন্তের দায়িত্ব দিলে এই বিবাদীপক্ষ ১১-১০-২০ ইং তারিখে অনিয়মের বিষয়ে তদন্ত করে প্রতিবেদন দাখিল করেন। ১ নং বিবাদীপক্ষ তার দাবীর সমর্থনে এলাকাবাসীর আবেদন, সরেজমিনে করা তদন্ত রিপোর্ট দাখিল করেছেন। উপরোক্ত আলোচনা এবং দাখিলী কাগজপত্র পর্যালোচনায় প্রতীয়মান হয় যে, নিষেধাজ্ঞার দরখাস্ত নামঞ্জুর হলে বাদীপক্ষের অপূরণীয় ক্ষতি হওয়ার কোন আশংকা নেই।"
<u>6. The learned Senior District Judge without assigning any cogent reason reversed the finding of the judgment and order of the learned Assistant Judge with the stroke of a pen. It is very unfortunate that the learned Senior District Judge without any independent and dispassionate consideration of the materials on record allowed the Miscellaneous Appeal and thereby committed an error of law causing serious failure of justice. The learned Senior District Judge observed:</u>
<u>"উভয়পক্ষকে অর্ন্তভুক্ত করিয়া যথাশীঘ্র নিরপেক্ষ, আইনানুগ ও অংশগ্রহণমূলক নির্বাচন অনুষ্ঠানের জন্য উপজেলা প্রাথমিক শিক্ষা অফিসার আশাশুনিকে এতদমর্মে নির্দেশ দেওয়া হইল।"</u>
7. The observation of the learned Senior District Judge enshrined in the operative portion of his judgment is unwanted and not based on sound reasoning.
<u>8. On perusal of the materials on record, I am of the view that the injunction petition is misconceived and the plaintiff did not come with clean hands and he has no locus standi to restrain the defendants from holding the Election of the Managing Committee of the said School. If such a petition is entertained, it will create obstruction or hindrance in the proper administration of the School.</u>
9. The learned Assistant judge rightly held that if the petition for temporary injunction is not granted, it will not cause any irreparable loss and injury to the plaintiff.
10. I am of the view that the balance of convenience and inconvenience is not in favour of the plaintiff, but it is in favour of the defendant; therefore, the impugned judgment and order of the learned Senior District judge is liable to be turned down to secure the ends of justice. Accordingly, I find substance in the Rule; hence, the Rule deserves to be made absolute.
11. In the result, the Rule is made absolute, without passing any order as to costs. The earlier of order of stay and status quo granted by this Court, thus, stands recalled and vacated.
12. The impugned judgment and order dated 1-4-2021 passed in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 5 of 2021 by the learned Senior District Judge, Satkhira is hereby set-aside and those of the learned Assistant Judge, Ashashuni, Satkhira passed in Title Suit No. 114 of 2020 is maintained.
13. The learned Assistant Judge, Ashashuni, Satkhira is directed to dispose of the original suit with utmost expedition preferably within 6 (six) months from the date of receipt of the copy of this judgment. No unnecessary adjournment shall be entertained from either side.
Let a copy of the judgment be transmitted to the Courts below at once.
End.
